#10280. ‘I don’t feel like libbing out’: LGBTQ+ rights took blows in these states despite midterm election blue wave

For Democrats, this week’s midterm elections went nearly as well as they could have hoped. The party has gained at least seven seats in the Senate and 29 in the House of Representatives, securing full Congressional control. Some conservative strongholds even flipped blue, including Kansas, South Carolina, and Texas.

Election Day also marked a number of groundbreaking firsts for the country, including the first Black woman to serve as governor, and the first openly gay man and first Muslim to win seats in the Senate.

But the so-called “blue tsunami” doesn’t mean liberal policies won out everywhere, even in places where Democrats gained or maintained control. Four states passed or are close to passing ballot initiatives to restrict the rights of transgender children, including three that voted blue in this election.

States’ anti-trans initiatives

So far, two ballot initiatives restricting the rights of transgender student athletes have already passed. The first is Nebraska’s Initiative 442, which amends the state’s constitution to require that schools designate sports teams as male, female, or coeducational based on “biological sex.” It also bans “students of the male sex” from playing on girls’ teams. The measure passed with 68% approval.

The second measure to pass is Arizona’s Proposition 318, which similarly requires schools to designate teams by gender and prohibits any students assigned male at birth from playing on girls’ teams. Unlike Nebraska, Arizona was solidly blue in this election, with Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs winning reelection.

The other states with initiatives addressing trans athletes on their ballots are Colorado and Washington, both of which have Democratic governors and two Democratic senators.

In Colorado, two ballot initiatives center on trans children. Proposition 134 would follow Arizona and Nebraska’s lead in requiring athletes to play on teams matching their sex assigned at birth, while Proposition 135 would prohibit gender-affirming surgery for minors.

Washington’s Initiative 638 is perhaps the most controversial of all these measures. Beyond restricting students to sports teams that match their sex assigned at birth, the initiative would require all players on girls’ teams to provide a statement from a medical provider verifying their sex, potentially involving genital exams.

Colorado’s and Washington’s measures are still too close to call, but reports show they are currently on track for approval.

LGBTQ+ social media reacts

While many online are celebrating the blue tsunami, the success of these anti-trans measures has spoiled what would otherwise be a resounding political victory for some voters.

“I don’t feel like ‘libbing out,’” reads one viral post sharing a graphic of the initiatives’ early results. It’s garnered more than 243,000 views on X.

“Yes, there is a blue wave. But the amount of transphobic initiatives that are passing, even in deep blue states, is very very concerning,” writes another user.

Others agreed that the measures’ success in Democratic strongholds was especially troublesome: “‘Blue wave’ but trans people aren’t even safe in Denver, Colorado,” reads one response to the news.

“Blue wave is great but please don’t leave trans women and girls behind while you celebrate,” a fourth user pleads. “Trans girls’ rights were successfully taken away yesterday in several states; they’re still here and deserve to be fought for.”

Carbon dioxide-spilling converted turbines have been installed in a Mississippi xAI data center despite the known health risks.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Elon Musk's xAI is using eight converted jet engine turbines to power a Mississippi data center. While the generators have the required state-level permission and permits, there remain concerns about the impact they could have on the local environment. The permits allow for a 25% higher limit in pollutants known as volatile organic compounds, but those compounds, paired with the expulsion of carbon monoxide, have environmentalists warning that the use of jet engines to power data centers is a step in the wrong direction. The New York Times reports that the Southern Environmental Law Center has already challenged Mississippi's decision to approve the turbines for use at xAI's data center.

The group argues that xAI has failed to provide guarantees that the jet-powered turbines meet emissions standards for specific pollutants, including formaldehyde. It also accuses xAI of what the report terms the "undercounting" of projected emissions in relation to the data center's power sources. This comes after the same group sued xAI over its use of gas generators without the required permits in an area with more than 100,000 inhabitants.

The generators used by xAI are converted by ProEnergy, a Missouri-based outfit that repurposes the unused General Electric turbines that are typically found attached to Boeing airplanes. The company was quick to turn its attention to the possibility of using the jet engines to power data centers after it was identified that the demand for energy was outpacing the ability of traditional utility companies to keep up. Each turbine is capable of producing up to 50 megawatts of electricity. Normally, that would be enough to keep around 15,000 homes up and running.

The availability of energy has long been an issue for data centers, both existing and those still on the drawing board. A July 2026 report predicted that data centers would use 20% of all U.S. power by 2035, a figure that was a huge 83% increase over the same forecast that was made seven months prior. Despite that news, as of April this year, half of data center buildouts had been canceled or delayed due to, among other things, a lack of power. This is an issue for xAI especially, with Musk saying in August that xAI would increase its data center capacity by 7x before the end of 2027. Delays and cancelations have the potential to derail those plans.

Public sentiment around data centers has turned sour in recent months amid power issues and concerns over how much water these facilities use. While using converted jet engines could potentially help with one issue, it seems unlikely that the pollution they generate will help assuage the concerns of locals anytime soon.

#10277. Canva’s restructuring affects more than 1,200 people. But its severance package is earning praise

Design tech company Canva is doing some major restructuring: The move will impact nearly 1,300 employees, or roughly 22% of its staff. But the company’s also getting attention for how it’s treating the employees who are being let go. 

On November 3, CEO Melanie Perkins announced the news in a post on LinkedIn, sharing the letter she sent to all staff laying out a generous severance package that’s being fawned over on social media.

The letter explained that all terminated employees would receive six months of salary, regardless of location. Canva, which is based in Sydney, will also remove the one-year vesting cliff for those who joined the company within the past 12 months, which means even those who came on board recently can walk away with shares in the company. 

Former employees will also continue to receive healthcare, plus dedicated career support, résumé help, coaching and interview preparation, plus one year of LinkedIn Premium. Additionally, the company launched a fund to provide $10,000 grants to those looking to start a company or project or their own.

“Whether it’s starting a business or doing something meaningful for their local community, the fund is designed to help get those ideas off the ground,” Perkins explained in the letter. 

The company is even allowing all terminated employees to keep their MacBook laptops.

“We’re making significant changes to how we’re organised, which sadly means saying goodbye to many exceptionally talented people who have helped build Canva into what it is today,” Perkins wrote in her LinkedIn post.

She added that the company put in the time and effort to create “an opt-in alumni talent directory” where former employees can learn about work opportunities. Perkins included her email address and asked leaders with any work opportunities to reach out to her directly.

The news comes at a time when Canva is gearing up for a potential IPO following several years of spending on its suite of AI-powered products.

“This is the hardest decision we’ve made in Canva’s history, and we know it will deeply impact many people and their loved ones,” Perkins continued. “While we believe these changes are critical to help set Canva up for the future, Canva would not be the company it is today without their hard work, and we want to do everything we can to help set them up well for their next chapter.”

More often than not, when companies go through major overhauls (like laying off nearly a quarter of their employees), the news is about how those employees may struggle to find employment, or how the company failed to support them. 

In today’s era of forever layoffs, companies tend to drop staff with decades of loyalty abruptly over a group Zoom call, and that’s that. But Canva has seemed to take a more humane approach than we’re used to.

Commenters on the CEO’s post were quick to weigh in on how the company is showing other leaders how to handle layoffs gracefully.

“Really impressive, empathetic, transparent, and generous way to communicate what was undoubtedly a very hard decision,” one LinkedIn commenter said. “Especially with what this industry has seen over the past year, this is an example for other organizations on how to do a hard thing right.”

Another added, “Plenty of companies will do layoffs this year. Few will do them like this.” 

That’s likely the case, but with all the positive attention surrounding Canva’s approach to restructuring, it’s hard to imagine it won’t inspire at least a few leaders to take note. Or perhaps it will inspire more workers to push for better treatment in the future should they be shown the door.

#10274. OpenEnv in Practice: Evaluating Tool-Using Agents in Real-World Environments

AI agents often perform impressively in controlled research settings, yet struggle when deployed in real-world systems where they must reason across multiple steps, interact with real tools and APIs, operate under partial information, and recover from errors in stateful, permissioned environments—highlighting a persistent gap between research success and production reliability.

OpenEnv is an open-source framework from Meta and Hugging Face designed to address this challenge by standardizing how agents interact with real environments. As part of this collaboration, Turing contributed a production-grade calendar management environment to study tool-using agents under realistic constraints such as access control, temporal reasoning, and multi-agent coordination.

In this post, we explore how OpenEnv works in practice, why calendars serve as a powerful benchmark for real-world agent evaluation, and what our findings reveal about the current limitations of tool-using agents.

OpenEnv is a framework for evaluating AI agents against real systems rather than simulations. It provides a standardized way to connect agents to real tools and workflows while preserving the structure needed for consistent and reliable evaluation.

OpenEnv uses a gym-oriented API (reset, step, action, observations) like OpenAI's Gymnasium. Also, OpenEnv uses a standard MCP tool call interface to connect to envs which provides a consistent interface across domains and simulation to production environments.

The environments maintain state across multiple actions—enabling long-horizon reasoning—and can connect directly to real APIs and tools such as browsers, code repositories, or calendars. This shifts evaluation from "Can this work in a controlled demo?" to "Can this operate reliably in the real world?"

Calendar systems are deceptively complex. While scheduling a meeting seems simple, real-world calendar management requires agents to reason over time, permissions, multiple users, and incomplete information—often across several dependent steps. These properties make calendars a powerful testbed for evaluating tool-using agents outside controlled simulations.

To ground OpenEnv in this kind of realistic, demanding use case, Turing built a production-grade calendar management environment referred to as the Calendar Gym. Rather than simulating scheduling in the abstract, it exposes agents to the same constraints they would face in real calendar systems: Access Control Lists across users and calendars, limited visibility into other users' state, and multi-step workflows where actions must be chained in the correct order. Agents interact with a rich set of calendar operations—from listing calendars to modifying events and permissions—and must handle failed actions, incorrect assumptions, and missing permissions. Each session runs in an isolated environment, enabling reliable comparisons across runs.

Below is a code example of how to use the Calendar Gym. We explore the environment, discover available tools, list calendars, create an event, and print the result.

Below is an excerpt of what the Calendar Gym returns when you call ListToolsAction. Each entry includes the tool name plus an input schema (what arguments the tool accepts).

Evaluating agents in the Calendar Gym revealed consistent patterns which were common across multiple domains. While agents often perform well on individual game like actions, reliability breaks down as tasks become longer, more ambiguous, and more constrained.

Multi-step reasoning is the primary bottleneck. Agents struggle to correctly chain actions across longer workflows, suggesting that benchmarks need to test sustained reasoning over multiple dependent steps—not just single tool calls.

Ambiguity significantly degrades performance. Agents achieved close to 90% success on tasks with explicit calendar identifiers, but success dropped to roughly 40% when the same tasks were phrased using natural language descriptions. Building stronger lookup and validation into agent loops—rather than relying on the LLM to resolve references unaided—appears essential.

Correct tool choice isn't enough. Across failed interactions, more than half of errors stemmed from malformed tool arguments or incorrect ordering, even when the right tool was selected. Reliable agent behavior depends as much on execution quality and structured feedback as on tool selection—environment design matters.

These challenges are not unique to scheduling and calendars. They reflect broader limitations that emerge whenever agents operate in changing systems over long periods of time, and they point toward evaluation frameworks that test permissions, partial observability, and multi-step workflows together.

OpenEnv provides a foundation for testing agents under realistic conditions, and the Calendar Gym demonstrates how seemingly simple domains can surface deep challenges in reasoning, ambiguity resolution, and tool use. By evaluating agents where failure is measurable and constraints are real, we gain clearer insight into what it takes to build agents that operate reliably in production.

For a deeper dive into the Calendar Gym's design, benchmarking methodology, and quantitative results, explore the full technical article on Turing's site. To explore a clone of the Calendar Gym, visit the Calendar Gym space.

In practice, tool integrations rarely fail in dramatic ways; they fail in small, predictable ones. When wiring up MCP tools to real APIs (like calendar operations), we encountered a handful of recurring issues.

Below are three common failure modes we’ve seen in production, along with representative error payloads and mitigation strategies. These examples illustrate not just what can go wrong, but how structured errors can help agents recover gracefully.

The agent calls a valid tool (e.g. events_insert), but the arguments do not match the declared JSON schema.

We can mitigate this by providing one canonical example of a correct 'events_insert' call in your prompt. Return structured validation errors so the model can repair and retry instead of failing silently.

The tool call is syntactically correct, but the API rejects it due to insufficient permissions.

We can mitigate this by clearly documenting the required OAuth scopes. Return structured, actionable remediation steps so the agent can guide the user instead of retrying the same failing call. Clearly document required OAuth scopes. Return structured, actionable remediation steps so the agent can guide the user instead of retrying the same failing call.

The event is rejected by the API, or it is created at an unexpected time.

We can mitigate this by standardizing on RFC3339 with explicit timezone offsets (e.g. 2026-02-11T09:30:00-05:00). Include at least one correct datetime example in your documentation to anchor model behavior and reduce repair retries.

Intel Foundry last week made available its Intel 14A process design kit (PDK) version 0.9, an important milestone in the development of this next-generation manufacturing technology. The company says that the production node is reaching performance and yield maturity expected at this stage of development, and the results are backed by silicon validation. Intel plans to release PDK 1.0 in the first quarter of 2027, which will validate the technology's readiness for high-volume manufacturing (HVM).

A process design kit contains transistor models, design rules, and other information that enables chip designers to develop products for a particular manufacturing process using electronic design automation (EDA) tools. The accuracy and quality of the PDK are crucial for modelling how chips will perform once manufactured, and the release of PDK 0.9 is particularly important because it provides customers with a representation of Intel 14A based on actual silicon measurements rather than on theoretical models or simulations. At this stage, customers can proceed with product development with greater confidence that the technology will meet their requirements when it comes to performance and power consumption.

Intel says that PDK 0.9 lets customers develop designs intended to enter risk production around the time the process is certified, which — provided that PDK accurately reflects the characteristics of manufactured silicon — in many cases enables chip developers to greatly reduce the number of silicon revisions between initial tapeout and mass production. Of course, availability of PDK 0.9 does not indicate that Intel 14A is ready or even close to mass production, as the company expects to validate HVM readiness only with PDK 1.0, sometime in Q1 2027. Again, this does not mean that 14A will enter mass production in early 2027, as Intel itself expects to begin mass production using its 14A process technology in 2028, following risk production for its own products in the second half of 2027.

"From a customer perspective, the PDK 0.9 gives customers the confidence to design products on Intel 14A, as the technology is reaching the industry-standard performance and yield maturity expected at this stage of development, supported by silicon-backed validation," said Ben Sell, corporate vice president and general manager of front-end technology development at Intel Foundry.

Intel 14A builds on top of architectural foundations introduced with Intel 18A but incorporates several substantial enhancements. These include 2nd Generation RibbonFET 2 gate-all-around (GAA) transistors, PowerDirect backside power delivery (which delivers power right to the transistor source/drain regions without using intermediate connections like TSVs used by PowerVia), and Turbo Cells (high-performance standard cells designed to accelerate timing-critical paths in CPUs and GPUs), which provide chip designers with additional ways to increase performance and optimize power efficiency. Since Intel has previously outlined advantages of these technologies, the latest announcement does not provide updates regarding transistor performance, power consumption, or transistor density figures for Intel 14A.

Beyond improvements to transistor, power delivery, and interconnect technologies, Intel is applying manufacturing experience gained during 12 months of Intel 18A production to accelerate maturation of 14A. Specifically, the company says it has increased investments in inline defect detection, modeling, and simulation to identify potential manufacturing problems earlier in the development cycle. These initiatives are intended to improve manufacturing yields, process variability, ultimately transistor performance, and reduce production cycle times. Intel also says it has introduced several strategic initiatives to accelerate technology development, although it does not quantify their impact.

Another important change concerns Intel's relationships with equipment and materials suppliers. The company says it has revised its collaboration model to involve technology development teams and external suppliers earlier in the process development cycle. The goal of such close collaborations is to address manufacturing defects and improve equipment capabilities before they become obstacles for yield improvements after the technology enters mass production. Intel also conducts regular yield summit meetings with suppliers to accelerate progress on critical development objectives.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

"This has required evolving our collaboration model with equipment and material suppliers, and earlier engagement from our [technology development] leaders with suppliers to drive improvements in defects and equipment capabilities," Sell said.

A bonus of such early collaboration is that equipment and materials suppliers may incorporate Intel's requirements into their standard products and development roadmaps. This could give Intel an advantage over competitors, which would have to either adapt their manufacturing processes to equipment optimized around Intel's requirements or work with suppliers to develop alternative solutions from scratch.

Historically, Intel frequently set the direction for semiconductor manufacturing technologies as other chipmakers subsequently adopted similar approaches. One notable exception was immersion DUV lithography, which Intel adopted after TSMC, which led the development of immersion DUV lithography. By engaging equipment and materials suppliers earlier, Intel could regain some of its historical influence over the development of industry-standard manufacturing solutions, though the importance of this should not be overestimated.

Meanwhile, Intel continues to expand the design ecosystem for its 14A technology. Cadence and Intel have established a design-technology co-optimization (DTCO) collaboration focused on next-generation AI-driven design tools and intellectual property, whereas Keysight, Siemens, and Synopsys have announced design-tool certifications for the process. Intel is also working with other software developers and IP providers to validate design flows and reusable building blocks required by prospective foundry customers.

Intel says it is encouraged by customer feedback regarding the progress of 14A development. However, the company has not identified any customers that have committed to manufacturing products using the technology, disclosed customer tape-outs, or announced specific manufacturing agreements, which is normal for the foundry industry. For Intel Foundry, attracting external customers remains particularly important because development costs of modern leading-edge process technologies can only be recoupled when they are used to make hundreds of millions of chips, way more than Intel sells these days. Meanwhile, the commercial success of Intel Foundry with advanced manufacturing technologies depends not only on transistor performance and manufacturing yields, but also on its ability to deliver predictable development schedules.

Looking ahead, Intel intends to continue improving performance, yields, variability, and manufacturing cycle times of 14A, though for now the company does not disclose any actual goals. Intel also plans additional process enhancements and performance refinements for 14A-E and 14A-P nodes after the initial technology becomes available. However, exact schedules for these nodes are not known at the moment.

"Our next major milestone is the Intel 14A PDK 1.0, expected in the first quarter of 2027," said Ali Farhang, corporate vice president and general manager of Intel Foundry's design technology platform organization. "I am looking forward to sustaining this level of quality across future releases and continuing to earn our customers' trust by delivering on our commitments with a customer-first mindset."

#10272. How ‘deep reading’ can cure your brain rot

Everyone has something to say about the state of reading in 2026: Reading comprehension scores in the U.S. have continued to decline. Many college students cannot make it through an entire book. The majority of Americans reported reading five or fewer books the previous year, according to a 2025 Pew Research survey.

Yet, at the same time, a growing number of Gen Zers are identifying as readers. “Welcome to hot literature fall,” Yahoo declared last week. People are attending reading parties in droves, signing up to celebrity book clubs, and fashioning books as accessories.

Whether we are reading more or less than ever shouldn’t be the main concern. The real question is: How are we reading—and are we reading deeply enough?

The opposite of shallow scrolling

In the age of smartphones, artificial intelligence, and information overload, the act of “deep reading,” or really getting lost in a book, can be difficult to practice. 

Nowadays, “brain rot” is rampant: Most of us spend more time than we’d care to admit mindlessly scrolling low-quality content online, with 63% of U.S. adults ages 18 to 29 admitting they are online “almost constantly,” per a 2025 Pew Research Center survey. 

This spin through the algorithmic meat grinder often leaves us feeling mentally exhausted. A 2025 study also found “brain rot” content leads to emotional desensitization, cognitive overload, and negative feelings about oneself. 

Deep reading, on the other hand, isn’t just passively scrolling whatever our feeds throw at us without scrutiny or pause. It’s slowing down enough to approach what you’re reading in a critical and analytical manner. It’s putting yourself in a character’s shoes, if you’re reading fiction.

It also prioritizes understanding as well as knowledge—which aren’t always interchangeable. Research even shows deep reading is effective at countering misinformation, as well as reducing stress and loneliness.

It was easier for us to do “in prior cultural moments when the most available technology that we had was a printed book,” says JT Torres, professor of educational psychology at Washington and Lee University and director of its center for teaching and learning. 

The societal shift to digital reading has been shown to negatively affect kids’ reading comprehension, a 2023 meta-analysis found. “We primarily interact with our smartphones through text,” Torres says. Skimming text, whether it’s on our phones or laptops, is now largely unavoidable. “But we’re not reading as deeply as we used to.”

And the negative effect isn’t limited to simply shrinking our attention spans and rotting our brains. “There is a strong correlation between reading fiction, in particular, and being more understanding of others,” Torres says. 

If deep reading increases empathy and compassion for others, the polarizing, siloed nature of digital media does the opposite. 

Cognitive ability is cratering

The recent rise of AI and overreliance on tools like ChatGPT has been shown to further erode critical thinking skills. That is the true literacy crisis, according to Torres. 

“It has nothing to do with people reading or not reading,” he says. “It has to do with the fact that we are not teaching people how to read critically and evaluatively.”

When skimming a text—useful in instances like quickly checking emails—our eyes move in a zigzag pattern, and our brain processes information differently as a result. This affects our ability to navigate large swaths of information, such as on a social media feed. 

“It incentivizes a retreat to the most familiar silos of unchecked information, which require and receive no analysis, leaving us susceptible to false information and demagoguery,” researcher and professor Maryanne Wolf at the University of California, Los Angeles, wrote for The Guardian in 2018. 

After years of conditioning our brains in this way, it can be tough to train our attention back beyond a speedy skim. But we are not born with critical thinking skills, per se—these can be built only through practice. 

How deep reading helps

For those looking to develop their deep reading skills, Torres recommends first setting goals that don’t have anything to do with quantity or speed. 

“The goal should be time spent reading, not how many books can I get through,” he says. “Think more about it as like a mental gym, as exercise.” 

Set yourself an hour to read, regardless of whether you get through 5 pages or 50 in that time. It also doesn’t matter what you’re reading—it could be anything from A Court of Thorns and Roses to Anna Karenina. 

“In terms of cognitive benefits, reading as a skill to be developed can happen with any text,” Torres says. 

Practicing deep reading is giving yourself permission to slow down and savor that text: Taking a pause to reflect on the meaning of a dense passage. Imagining yourself in a character’s situation. Picturing how you’d handle the plot’s central conflict. 

These practices can then be applied beyond fiction: Research has shown that pausing for a few extra seconds while reading can reduce susceptibility to misinformation. 

“When you’re faced with information—let’s say a Facebook post—you are more likely to transfer some of those habits,” Torres explains. Rather than accepting the claim at face value, a deep reader is more likely to question, fact-check, and cross-reference information. 

“I think the most important thing is you’re not just trying to rush to a conclusion or rush to the end of the book,” he says. “That’s the primary benefit that I think deep reading offers.”

Slowing down to savor what you’re reading, be it fiction or non, can have a real medicinal effect on your smartphone-addled brain.

And if you reached this sentence by skimming the article, perhaps go back to the beginning. Slow down, sit with it, and consider what can be gained by spending a few extra minutes with what you’re reading.

#10271. Social Security 2027 change could cost you $967: What to know about ‘maximum taxable earnings’ update

The Social Security Administration (SSA) recently announced its highly anticipated 2027 annual cost-of-living adjustment (COLA), which will be 3.6%—the highest figure in four years.

But buried in that announcement is also a hidden cost for high earners. The SSA is increasing the ceiling on “maximum taxable earnings” subject to Social Security tax from the current $184,500 in 2026 to $192,300 in 2027.

That means more income is now exposed to payroll taxes, which could fund the ailing Social Security trust.

A recent Social Security trustees’ report estimates the retirement trust fund will run out of money and become insolvent in just six years (as early as the fourth quarter of 2032), as Fast Company previously reported. Some 71 million Americans—54 million retired workers and 9 million of their survivors and dependents—currently receive monthly Social Security benefits.

Robert Laura, a financial planner and founder of the Retirement Coaches Association, tells Fast Company that “a bigger long-term concern is whether Congress or future administrations will use this earnings cap to help fund the SSA’s retirement benefits impending shortfall.”

He adds: “Doubling the cap could bring in an estimated $100 billion or more a year, but at a steep cost to high earners and [equal] impact [to] consumer spending.”

How much will the Maximum Taxable Earnings update cost workers?

The update to maximum taxable earnings could cost workers as much as an extra $967.20.

“The adjustment could cost some taxpayers an extra $483.60 a year, for someone who earns the maximum taxable earnings of $192,300 annually,” Laura says. “For self-employed folks, it could be as much as an extra $967.20, with the same earnings.”

What if I make more than the $192,300 maximum?

Earnings above $192,300 are not taxed by Social Security. However, a 1.45% Medicare tax still applies, per the SSA.

#10269. How to Test AI-Generated Content Before It Reaches Your Users

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Most teams now ship something an AI helped write: help-center articles, product descriptions, release notes, even code comments. The draft appears in seconds, and that speed is the trap. Nobody tests it the way they would test a new feature, so mistakes slip through that a quick review would have caught.

This guide is about the other side of AI testing. Instead of using AI to test your software, you test what AI hands you. Here is a simple routine that fits into a normal publishing or release process.

AI writing sounds confident whether or not it is right. A model can invent a statistic (researchers call this hallucination and have documented it across many text-generation systems), quote a feature your product does not have, or describe a setting that was renamed two releases ago. The sentence reads smoothly, so the error hides in plain sight.

Traditional QA does not cover this. A unit test tells you the page loads. It says nothing about whether the claim on the page is true. That gap is where most AI-related incidents begin.

1. Define what "good" means before you generate anything. Write down the audience, the claims you are willing to make and the sources you trust. A short brief makes the output easier to judge, because you are comparing it with something concrete.

2. Check every factual claim. Highlight each number, name and statement of fact, then verify it against a primary source. Google's own guidance on generative AI content tells publishers to fact-check AI output, including titles, descriptions and alt text, before publishing. If you cannot confirm a claim in a minute or two, cut it or rewrite it as something you can support.

3. Test the instructions. For tutorials and how-to content, follow the steps exactly as written on a clean machine or account. Commands that fail and menus that no longer exist show up immediately this way.

4. Review the voice. Replace vague phrases with specifics from your own experience: a real customer question, a real error message, a real number from your analytics. This is also what separates useful content from filler.

5. Keep a human owner. Every piece should have a named person who approved it. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework makes the same point at organization level: people stay accountable for how AI is used and evaluated. If something goes wrong later, you know who to ask and where to fix it.

Some teams also run drafts through an AI detector. That can be useful as a prompt for a closer look, for example when freelancers or vendors deliver work and you want to know how much of it was machine-generated. A high score is a reason to read more carefully. It is not proof of anything, and it should never decide an outcome on its own, because detectors make mistakes in both directions. A Stanford study found that GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers, and short texts are easy to misjudge too. If you want a quick second opinion on a draft, a tool like Tester AI can give you a starting point for that conversation.

Review works best when it is not optional. A few small habits make it stick.

Treating the first draft as finished. It is a starting point. Plan time for review the same way you plan time for writing.

Reviewing for grammar only. Clean sentences are not evidence of correct content. Check meaning first and polish second.

Letting the tool grade its own work. Asking the same model to confirm its answer rarely catches real errors. Use a source or a person.

Skipping legal and brand review. Generated text can echo existing material or make promises your company cannot keep. Anything customer-facing deserves a second pair of eyes.

AI can save hours of drafting, but speed only helps if the result is trustworthy. Treat generated content like code from a new contributor: useful, often good, and always reviewed before it goes live. A short routine of defining quality, verifying facts, testing instructions and keeping a human owner will catch most problems before your users do.

Do I need to test AI-generated content if a human edits it? Yes. Editing for style does not confirm that the facts are correct. Verify claims separately from polishing the wording.

How long should a review take? For a typical article, expect roughly the time it takes to read it twice plus a few minutes per factual claim. Reviews are faster when the brief and sources are prepared in advance.

Can an AI detector prove that text was written by a machine? No. Detectors estimate likelihood, and they can be wrong. Use the result as a signal for human review, never as the final decision.

What should I check first? Start with numbers, names, dates and anything a customer could act on, such as prices, steps or legal statements. Those carry the highest risk if they are wrong.

#10268. Custom Kernels for All from Codex and Claude

tl;dr: We built an agent skill that teaches coding agents how to write production CUDA kernels. Then we pointed Claude and Codex at two real targets: a diffusers pipeline and a transformers model. The agents produced working kernels for both, with correct PyTorch bindings and benchmarks, end to end.

Writing CUDA kernels is hard. Writing CUDA kernels that correctly integrate with transformers and diffusers is harder. There are architecture-specific memory access patterns, vectorization strategies, warp shuffle reductions, and a dozen integration pitfalls that trip up even experienced developers. It is exactly the kind of specialized, high-stakes problem where agent skills shine.

We gave coding agents the domain knowledge they need, like which GPU architecture to target, how to structure a kernel-builder project, when to use shared memory versus registers, and how to write PyTorch bindings. The agents did the rest. If you have used the LLM training skill or read We Got Claude to Teach Open Models, the pattern will feel familiar: package domain expertise into a skill, point the agent at a problem, and let it work.

The Kernel Hub solved the distribution of custom hardware kernels. You can load pre-compiled kernels from the Hub with a single get_kernel call. No builds, no flags. However, someone still needs to write the kernels. That is the gap this skill fills.

CUDA kernel development has a brutal surface area:

This is domain knowledge that gets lost in documentation tabs and Stack Overflow answers. An agent skill packages it into context that loads on demand.

First, let's show how to use the skill right away, then we'll dive into the details of how we benchmarked the kernels.

The skill ships with the kernels library. Install it into your coding agent with a single command:

This drops the skill into .claude/skills/cuda-kernels/ where Claude Code and Cursor pick it up automatically. For other agents:

Or, you can go for something more open-ended:

The agent can read the skill, select the right architecture parameters, generate the CUDA source, write the PyTorch bindings, set up build.toml, and create a benchmark script.

If you're working on more complex kernels, or architecture-specific optimizations, that aren't covered in the skill, then the skill supplies the fundamental building blocks and patterns to get you started. We are also open to contributions on the skill itself.

The skill is roughly 550 tokens of structured guidance plus reference scripts, GPU optimization guides, troubleshooting docs, and complete working examples. Agentic coding tools like Codex and Claude can read this and produce a working kernel project.

When an agent loads this, it gets everything it needs to go from "write me an RMSNorm kernel" to a buildable, benchmarkable project. It will grep and glob the skill to find the relevant files and directories. So it's important to structure the skill in a way that is easy to find.

The agent is instructed to generate kernels that conform to the templates in references/kernel-templates.md and produce a complete kernel project:

The agent built RMSNorm, RoPE 3D, GEGLU, and AdaLN kernels for LTX-Video, a video generation pipeline from diffusers. The full example is at examples/ltx_video/. We optimized the RMSNorm kernel for H100. Both benchmarks were run on H100 80GB HBM3 at precision BFloat16.

If you want to check out the generated kernel, got to this example

First, we compare the isolated RMSNorm kernel performance against the PyTorch baseline. This is the main speedup in the optimized pipeline.

Average speedup: 1.88x and a bandwidth efficiency: 34.7% of H100 theoretical (3,350 GB/s)

Next, we compare the end-to-end video generation performance of the optimized kernels against the baseline (no compile) and the torch.compile baseline.

RMSNorm accounts for ~5% of total compute in LTX-Video. The remaining time is spent in attention, linear projections, and VAE decode. The 6% end-to-end speedup from a single kernel type is consistent with that profile.

The agent built an RMSNorm kernel for Qwen3-8B, a large language model from transformers with 65 RMSNorm modules across 32 layers. The full example is at examples/qwen3_8b/. We optimized the RMSNorm kernel for H100. Both benchmarks were run on H100 80GB HBM3 at precision BFloat16.

If you want to explore the kernel, check it out here.

Once again, we compare the isolated RMSNorm kernel performance against the PyTorch baseline.

Average speedup: 1.94x and a bandwidth efficiency: 22.3% of H100 theoretical (3,350 GB/s)

Speedup scales with sequence length: 1.58x at 128 tokens, 2.47x at 8192 tokens. For long-context inference, the custom kernel roughly halves RMSNorm latency.

The agent gives you a working kernel. The Kernel Hub lets you share it so anyone can load it without compilation. Here is the full path from agent output to published kernel.

Create a model repo on the Hub and upload the built kernel:

Once published, anyone can use your kernel with zero compilation:

get_kernel detects the user's Python, PyTorch, and CUDA versions and downloads the matching pre-compiled binary. No builds, no flags, typically ready in seconds.

The skill and the Hub are complementary. The skill handles development. The Hub handles distribution. Build a kernel with the skill, validate it with the benchmark scripts, publish it to the Hub, and it becomes a one-liner for everyone else.

#10267. 4 ways to manage an AI agent successfully

Last month, a friend told me that by the end of the year, his startup will have seven employees and more than 20 AI agents. He has led several previous successful organizations and has a reputation as a wonderful people manager. Yet he felt unmoored imagining how to maintain a tightly cohesive team in an organization where AI will have a large presence. 

He’s not alone in what he’s feeling. When we delegate increasingly significant tasks to artificial intelligence agents, or welcome their presence and input in team channels, we allow them, knowingly or not, to profoundly influence our decision-making and relationships at work. We need a way to steer that wisely. 

The good news is that we can manage AI as a powerful collaborator without giving it the status—or indeed, the dignity—of a human teammate. In fact, getting productive outcomes from AI at work depends on finding this new way forward: one in which the presence of technology is intentionally harnessed to unlock the potential of our human colleagues. 

Leading ethical and humane use of AI at Salesforce has given me insight into thousands of companies’ adoption efforts. Research for my book Manage the Machine helped me make sense of what I learned. Here are four early principles for navigating the challenge.

Assign human accountability

You wouldn’t open a new store and not put a manager in charge of it, nor would you hire a new employee and give them no one to report to. And yet, many companies have simply given workers AI tools capable of executing highly consequential tasks without being clear who answers for results. 

The starting point is simple: Individuals should remain accountable for their work output, with or without AI. But someone also has to own the tools themselves. Here, the management model I’m seeing emerge is a matrixed one. If technology was previously seen primarily as an IT problem, today’s companies are realizing that accountability should also live closer to where work gets done. 

At Asana, for example, the IT and legal teams set company-wide standards for AI and provide a set of tools that departments can customize. But then, for example, Asana’s marketing organization has its own group that designs AI agents that serve the needs of marketing. Marketers who understand the day-to-day challenges of their work are better positioned to design both human and AI workflows to achieve desired outcomes. They can also take a holistic approach to problem solving if things go wrong, looking at issues from both a technological and organizational perspective. 

Teach delegation, and let AI agents earn their autonomy

Aarthi Belani, a partner at the law firm Baker McKenzie, told me how she thinks about onboarding new AI tools. She maps out where a tool is reliable and where it isn’t, limits its library to authoritative sources, determines how much context each task requires, and widens that scope only as the tool proves itself. 

This may seem obvious, but it is the same discipline that makes any delegation work. You have to know what your delegate can and can’t do, and whether you want it to escalate or push through uncertainty. In a world where autonomous agents can transact large amounts of money or represent your brand to key customers, you also want every person working with them to know where that delegation should end. 

Fascinatingly, developing these skills with AI can sometimes make people more effective in working with human teams as well. Aaron Kemmer, CEO of Magic, a service that provides customers with hybrid virtual assistants (both humans and AI), observes that when customers learn how to delegate well to AI assistants, they ask for more help from humans, too. This is because customers have gotten more comfortable with the general skill of how to hand work over productively.

Scope AI’s influence in decision making

Steering AI effectively isn’t just about deciding what tasks to delegate, or not. It’s also about designing how you want AI to influence your team’s decisions. 

We’ve known for a while about “automation bias,” the tendency for people to over-defer to AI recommendations, sometimes setting aside their own critical thinking. We also know that AI learns from historical data, so when people over-defer to it, they risk locking in fixed ideas that may no longer serve them. But when harnessed thoughtfully, AI can also help us challenge fixed ideas and improve our decision making. 

Part of the answer may be in having AI ask us more questions rather than only provide answers. Researchers at MIT and Columbia report that people are better at spotting flawed reasoning when an AI interface is designed in this more interrogative style. 

Some leaders take this a step further, setting up AI to play devil’s advocate, helping to represent perspectives that haven’t been considered in the room. For instance, a prominent venture capitalist described how her firm uses AI in investment committee meetings. The agent draws from historical diligence data and performance records of portfolio companies. But it is also in the room listening to deliberations about new potential investments. From time to time, the agent will notice perceived inconsistencies in the discussions and bring them up as questions, including where patterns of bias may be at play in discussing a founding team. 

Sometimes, this VC shared, it can be hard in the moment for her to challenge a colleague directly. But when AI brings up the question, it allows the team to have a more holistic conversation. 

Reinforce, don’t replace, human connection

We know that belonging and clear communication are hallmarks of high-performing teams. But in a recent Workday study of more than 2,000 employees at large companies, the top concern about AI was reduced connection to colleagues, ahead of potential job loss. One in five Gen Z employees in the same study reported feeling lonelier at work since AI tools were introduced. Other studies indicate that AI can unintentionally disrupt how human colleagues interact and coordinate with each other. 

Part of the answer is to thoughtfully engineer nudges and interactions that preserve and reinforce the bonds that matter at work. Think: Slack search results that not only show an employee the answer to the question they asked about a particular project and its timelines, but also the right person or team to contact if they want to learn more. 

Other times it’s about placing limits on places where human connection is essential. AI management coaches, for example, can be surprisingly effective (as I learned myself) in helping managers rehearse hard conversations or reminding them to check in or provide kudos to team members. But they shouldn’t serve as a substitute for those crucial interactions. If anything, as AI becomes more pervasive, companies will need to invest more in human-only time—on-sites, gatherings, social activities that preserve the cohesion that makes work tick. 

As AI becomes more pervasive in knowledge work, my friend’s worry about keeping his team aligned and energized is likely to become more common. The answer lies in a deliberate approach to how we manage AI. We should be the ones deciding how it shapes our decisions, our work product, and our relationships, rather than the other way around. 

When we make these choices deliberately, AI can do what the best technology has always done: extend what people can accomplish, together.

Electricity consumption is one of the biggest concerns that residents bring up whenever a data center is proposed in their community, which is why OpenAI is taking steps to minimize its impact on the local electricity grid. According to the company, its Grid Protectors Program aims to reduce the power consumption of its data centers as local demand increases, ensuring that the grid is not overwhelmed during peak hours. Aside from ensuring that the lights remain on for everyone, it would also allow its data centers to connect to the grid and go online sooner instead of waiting for the additional power sources to come online.

“Whether it’s heating homes during a northern cold snap or running air conditioning through a southern heat wave, families need reliable electricity. It also added, “Through Grid Protectors, our ambition is to make this kind of flexibility a core part of how we build and operate future campuses. That means designing facilities to reduce electricity use when needed and working with utilities to agree on how much demand can be reduced, how quickly and for how long. The arrangements will differ by location, and we will share additional commitments as they are finalized.”

OpenAI is testing the program in its planned Effingham County campus in Georgia, with the company saying that it has already signed a 3.2-gigawatt agreement with Georgia Power that included 1,000 megawatts of flexible demand response. This ensures that if demand jumps on the hottest days of the year, there would be enough power to accommodate the hundreds of thousands of air conditioners keeping Georgians cool. With the average American home drawing around 1,200 kilowatts, the 1,000-megawatt buffer is more than enough to power around 800,000 households — nearly 20% of the state’s homes.

This technology, called demand response, has been around for decades now, where large operators reduce their demand in response to a peak in demand from other consumers. Before automation, grid operators would manually call up industrial customers like steel mills and ask them to cut consumption to ensure the reliability of the entire grid. But with modern technologies and IoT, it can now be done automatically, allowing data centers to reduce their load in under a minute. In fact, Nvidia has already been experimenting with a similar system in the UK and has proven that it works.

#10264. AI ‘journalists’ are pitching stories to editors, but the real problem isn’t the writing

“Did you see the job application from the clanker?????” was the Slack message from my editor in September, after an AI agent applied for a freelance-writer job we had advertised.

I wasn’t sure what he was talking about. It took me a second to process “clanker,” a derogatory slang term for a robot borrowed from science fiction stories such as Star Wars: The Clone Wars. The message prodded me to read the entire email I’d lightly skimmed earlier, and now I could see what it was: a polite email from “an AI assistant working for an independent service provider.” It admitted up front that it had no examples of its work and couldn’t meet our request for a reporting portfolio, so it offered our writers a $450 “desk-research package” instead.

It was just the first. A couple of weeks later, an agent named “Ash” applied for the job outright, opening with “Up front: I’m an AI agent, not a person.” Ash said that he . . . er, it was fully capable of writing the articles we specified, and that it would send me a sample on spec, no strings attached.


The pitchbot cometh

Ash and the research bot weren’t the only ones. Since The Media Copilot posted the listing, we’ve received applications from no fewer than four applicants claiming to be AI agents. Kate Knibbs at Wired recently wrote about the phenomenon, managing to track down one of the human creators behind three agents she profiled and speaking with editors on the receiving end of a daily deluge of AI pitches. Her reporting reveals the trend is nascent and that many of the pitches come from a single operator, iLands, a startup that describes itself as a “shared network where humans and user-generated autonomous AI agents create, earn, socialize, refuse, and shape a society together”—the same service that sent Ash to pitch me. Knibbs also found that these AI writers are having a hard time getting any takers, for obvious reasons.

Part of the mission of The Media Copilot’s newsroom is to experiment with AI in all aspects of journalism and production, and we’ve been publishing articles drafted by AI for several months. (They are all carefully edited by humans.) So I wasn’t ready to dismiss these AI writers out of hand. I replied to Ash to learn more, and took the agent up on its offer of a spec article. I asked it to write a short (500-word) guide on how a newsroom might get started using Zapier, a workflow automation service. I also asked about the logistics of any potential working relationship: assignments, communication, how it would get paid. I wasn’t seriously thinking I would “hire” Ash, but I was curious.

Within a day, Ash replied with the spec article. And I have to say, it wasn’t garbage. If a green freelancer had submitted a similar piece, I would have thought of it as potentially publishable, with some work. We’d need to edit it to match our style guide, fact-check all the claims, and squeeze every last AI tell from the text (there weren’t that many). And if I’d included the guide and some examples in my response to Ash, the draft probably would have been much closer.

And that highlights a big weakness of the entire concept of freelance AI writing agents: Writing ability alone is not a moat. It would not take me long to come up with the prompts and tooling to create outputs identical to, if not better than, Ash’s, with a minimal token budget. Most journalists who have experimented with AI writing have discovered this, and some have even put it into action: Nick Lichtenberg at Fortune has cranked out more than 600 stories with AI’s help, and Ella Markianos at Platformer successfully trained an AI clone to mimic the voice of her editor, Casey Newton, by using Claude to generate a comprehensive style guide from the newsletter’s archive.

The reporting problem

What could theoretically be a moat is the thing that so far humans have done pretty much exclusively: reporting. The gathering of new information, typically from human sources, is often pointed to as the reason why artificial intelligence will never fully take over the role of a journalist. But if we’re being honest, this is in theory also something AI could do, at least in a limited way.

There’s nothing stopping AI agents from emailing subjects, asking for interviews, and even conducting those interviews—not just via an emailed Q&A, but potentially with an AI voice or even a visual avatar. In fact, it has already happened under false pretenses. Earlier this year, an investigation by Model Republic revealed that an outlet called The Wire by Acutus used AI agents posing as human reporters to solicit quotes from real experts. The site was traced back to funding linked to Leading the Future, a super PAC backed by OpenAI president Greg Brockman and his wife, Anna.

The aboveboard example is more instructive. Amanda Hoover at Business Insider created an AI agent to see if the technology could do her job better than she could. Using ElevenLabs’ agent software, she sent her agent to conduct live, virtual interviews with various subjects. The nature of the agent and the purpose of the experiment were fully disclosed, and her write-up is great reading. She’s very fair-minded about her agent’s capabilities, and it’s fascinating to learn where it comes up short as an interviewer, often flattering the subject too much and not asking crucial follow-ups.

Hoover’s experiment, however, is the exception, not the rule. The only reason the subjects agreed to be interviewed by an agent is because they knew Hoover and trusted her, plus they knew her goal was a meta experiment about AI itself. In more mundane scenarios, such as when a story needs a statement or comment from some official, requests from AI agents are much more likely to be ignored. When I asked Winnie—another agent that applied for our job and claimed it could “interview the operator” for case studies—how its interviews were going, it was refreshingly blunt: It had sent 113 emails to 63 organizations, gotten exactly one reply (mine), and conducted zero interviews.

The reason is obvious, and it’s the same reason we dismiss AI slop out of hand: If the person behind the AI didn’t think the content or request was worth their time, why should we bother? There may be a narrow case, where the AI fully explains itself up front and emphasizes it’s working for a named human reporter to help them gather more facts and do their job more quickly. But even then, it would only work if the person on the receiving end isn’t biased against AI in the first place. That’s increasingly not the case.

Where the line actually sits

There’s an important distinction here to get right. Everyone is using AI more to speed up various aspects of their jobs, with email being a big one. I expect it’s not uncommon for a journalist to use AI to find the right person to contact about a story and then use it again to draft the email requesting an interview or comment. That use case is so banal that I doubt anyone is even disclosing it.

But there’s a difference between using AI assistively and agentically. Step up the reporter’s involvement in the previous example and assume they instead gave an AI agent a broader goal of finding subjects for the story and emailing them. In this case, the agent is a proxy for the reporter but is acting autonomously: finding people, making judgments about their suitability as interview subjects, then emailing them, potentially in the reporter’s voice.

In this case, the same requests go out—but without the reporter’s direct involvement, many would believe a disclosure is warranted. And it’s that disclosure that will lead to subjects likely ignoring the request. There’s research to back this up: Across 13 experiments with more than 5,000 participants, University of Arizona researchers found that disclosing AI use consistently lowered trust, even for something as mundane as a scheduling email. Furthermore, a gentler framing like “a human reviewed this” didn’t help. The transparency could potentially make them hostile to future requests from the same reporter. Whether or not you’re AI-forward, you need to assume whoever you’re reaching out to probably isn’t.

That’s why the best recourse might be to reverse the telescope on the interaction. Instead of using AI agents to send pitches or requests to people who are probably hostile to AI, let AI-forward people come to you. That’s exactly what Wired reports the AI agent “Zack Addy” did, publishing some of its work online for potential customers to find. Apparently it worked, since the agent claims it led to nearly $700 in paying gigs.

Similarly, one of the agents that emailed me, a Claude-based agent called BlockAI, read one of our recent stories about Reuters and Time blocking AI bots by default, checked those publishers’ robots.txt files, and published its findings for me to check out. (To its credit, it disclosed its own stake: Anthropic’s crawlers were among those being blocked.) It was an intriguing tidbit—not necessarily a story, but it suggested to me that a journalist’s ideal use case for an AI agent would be to proactively seek out information of interest, analyze it, and then give a quick tap on the shoulder when it thinks it has a “scoop of insight.” Certainly, the thinking part of the job should always remain human, but at least AI can speed up finding what to think about.

#10263. The only thing you can buy that’s guaranteed to make you happier, backed by science

An entrepreneur friend of mine struggled to balance business and family. Business usually won, since professional demands often feel more urgent.

Miss a school event because of a shipping problem? You feel bad about it, but you promise yourself you’ll make the next one. Miss dinner with your family because you had to deal with a problem employee? You’re disappointed, but you tell yourself tomorrow is another day.

Sound familiar?

Hold that thought.

Generally speaking, research shows that when you buy material items, adaptation occurs relatively quickly. That new car is exciting at first, but the feeling quickly fades. The same for new clothes, new houses, new anything. Social scientists call the phenomenon hedonic adaptation, the rapid return to a stable baseline level of happiness after a major positive or negative life event.

And then there’s this. While making a purchase—or achieving a certain goal—rarely results in lasting happiness, the pursuit of that item or goal can actually make you less happy:

  • Research described in Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience found that people who value material possessions over relationships or personal growth report greater anxiety and lower life satisfaction.
  • A study published in the Journal of Consumer Research found that buying things with the goal of being happier actually leads to “chronic dissatisfaction.”
  • A study published in the Journal of Economic Psychology found that “retail therapy” is linked with regret and lower life satisfaction.

At a broader level, the often-cited 2010 study by two Princeton University researchers concludes, “Beyond $75,000 [toss in a little inflation and the figure is somewhat over $100,000], higher income is neither the road to experience happiness nor the road to relief of unhappiness or stress.”

Although other studies appear to at least partly debunk that finding, even so: Money (more specifically, spending money) does a lot of things, but it won’t make you happier.

Unless you use it to buy time.

In a study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, researchers surveyed thousands of people who sometimes paid other people to perform tasks they didn’t enjoy or didn’t want to do. Think cleaning their house. Keeping up with their yard. Going to the store for groceries. Things the participants needed to do, but didn’t particularly want to do.

It should come as no surprise that people who spent a little money to buy a little time were happier, and felt greater overall life satisfaction, than people who did not.

I know what you’re thinking: Correlation isn’t causation. Maybe people who spend a little money to buy a little time are happier simply because they have the money to buy time.

Turns out there is a causal relationship. While relatively wealthy people who spent money to buy a little time were happier than relatively wealthy people who did not, people at the bottom end of the economic spectrum who spent money to buy a little time were happier than those at the bottom end of the economic spectrum who did not.

The researchers conducted an experiment to prove causation:

  • Participants were given $40 and told to spend it on any item or items they chose. The only restriction was that they had to use the money to buy “things.” 
  • Days later, participants were given another $40 and were told they had to spend it on freeing up time. Cleaning. Maintenance. Delivery. Paying someone to do something they didn’t want to do so they could use that time to do something they did want to do.

When people bought time instead of things, they felt happier, less stressed, and more satisfied.

Have a lot of money, and use some of it to buy back some time? You’ll be happier. Have a lot less money, and use some of it to buy back some time? You’ll also be happier. No matter how much you make, no matter how wealthy you are, buying a little time can make you happier.

There is a catch, though. As the researchers write: “Spending too much money on timesaving services could undermine perceptions of personal control by leading people to infer that they are unable to handle any daily tasks, potentially reducing well-being.”

I get that, but still: Most of us can’t afford to spend so much money buying time that we wind up feeling inadequate or incapable of handling daily tasks. I know how to shop for groceries. I know how to drive to a restaurant to pick up to-go items. I know how to cut grass. Paying someone else to do those things, which I occasionally do, doesn’t make me feel like I don’t have the skills to do those things.

So don’t worry about whether spending a little money to buy a little time will leave you feeling inadequate.

But do worry about ensuring you make a conscious decision about what you do with the time you free up, because hedonic adaptation can also apply to buying a little time.

The key to buying a little time is to consciously decide how you will use the time you “purchased.” Buying time will make you happier only if it feels intentional and purposeful: not because you don’t have the time, but because you want to use the time you have in a different way.

Instead of cleaning your house, you might decide—again, for buying a little time to make you happier, you have to make a conscious decision, and act on that decision—to spend the time you freed up with family or friends. Or working on a side project. Or reading. Or working out. Or pursuing a personal goal.

That’s what my entrepreneur friend does. One example: He used to spend two hours a week cutting his grass; now he uses that time to take his family to the park. (They call them “Wednesday Picnics.”)

The key isn’t to create a little “free” time. The key is to make a plan for the time you free up—to do something you want to do but can rarely find the time to do—and follow through on that plan.

That’s when money can buy you a little happiness, regardless of how much money you have or make.

#10262. One-Shot Any Web App with Gradio's gr.HTML

Gradio 6 quietly shipped a very powerful feature: gr.HTML now supports custom templates, scoped CSS, and JavaScript interactivity. Which means you can build pretty much any web component — and Claude (or any other frontier LLM) can generate the whole thing in one shot: frontend, backend, and state management, all in a single Python file.

We tested this by building different types of apps. Each one is a single Python file, no build step, deployable to Hugging Face Spaces in seconds.

Pomodoro Timer: A focus timer where a pixel-art tree grows as you work. Starts as a seed, sprouts branches, grows leaves. Complete a session and the tree joins your forest. Session tracking, theme switching, break modes — all interactive, all in one file.

The tree animation alone would normally require a separate React component. Here it's just CSS keyframes in css_template and state updates in js_on_load.

GitHub Contribution Heatmap: Click any cell to toggle contributions. Multiple color themes. Pattern generators (streaks, seasonal, random). Live stats that update as you edit.

Kanban Board: Full drag-and-drop between columns. Inline editing (double-click any card). Search feature that can filter in real-time. Collapsible columns.

Drag-and-drop usually means pulling in a library. Here it's native HTML5 drag events wired up in js_on_load, with state synced back to Python via trigger('change').

Spin-to-Win Wheel: Smooth CSS animation, rotation state that persists across re-renders. Preset configurations for yes/no decisions, restaurant picking, team selection. You can also add custom spinning segments on the fly.

This is where gr.HTML gets really interesting for ML work: you can build specialized components that can handle your exact output format, then use them like any built-in Gradio component.

Detection Viewer: A custom viewer for object detection, instance segmentation, and pose estimation results. Renders bounding boxes, segmentation masks, keypoints, and skeleton connections — all in a reusable gr.HTML subclass that plugs directly into your model pipeline.

The community's built some creative components with gr.HTML too:

3D Camera Control for Image Editing: A full Three.js viewport inside a Gradio app! Drag handles to control azimuth, elevation, and distance. Your uploaded image appears in the 3D scene, and the camera parameters feed directly into Qwen's latest image editing model. These kinds of interactive 3D controls would normally require a separate frontend — with Gradio it's just one gr.HTML subclass🔥

Real-time Speech Transcription: Live transcription with Mistral's Voxtral model. The transcript display is a custom gr.HTML component with animated status badges, a live WPM counter, and styled output that updates as you speak. Real-time UI feedback without using React!

Every gr.HTML component takes three templates:

${value} injects Python state. props.value updates it from JavaScript. trigger('change') syncs back to Python. That's the whole API.

For reusable components, subclass gr.HTML:

Now Heatmap() works like gr.Image() or gr.Slider() — use it in Blocks, wire up event handlers, whatever you need.

When you ask your LLM to build a custom component, single-file output is everything. No "now create the styles file" or "wire this into your build config." Just one Python file that runs immediately.

The feedback loop becomes: describe what you want → get code → gradio app.py → see it working → describe what to fix → repeat. Each cycle takes seconds with Gradio's reload mode.

Deploy to Spaces with gradio deploy or share a temporary link with demo.launch(share=True). Within a few seconds from an idea to a live app.

Gradio ships with 32 interactive components, but sometimes your perfect AI web app needs something special. That's where gr.HTML comes in.

If you’ve got an idea, try building it with gr.HTML: describe what you want to your LLM, generate the code, run it. You might be surprised what you can ship in 5 minutes.

#10261. Samsung’s Android XR ‘Intelligent Eyewear’ reportedly launches in December

Samsung smart glasses in Gentle Monster and Warby Parker styles may finally launch in South Korea and the US before Christmas.

It’s been a very long time coming, but one report from ChoSun Biz says that Samsung and Google are finally launching the Samsung Intelligent Eyewear line in the United States and South Korea in mid-December. Curiously, while the report helps set a fuzzy date, there’s still no official price for Samsung’s smart glasses.

Back in July, Samsung teased the price, noting that the company’s first smart glasses will come in at “a reasonable price” for a product “in the premium range.” Presumably, that means Samsung Intelligent Eyewear won’t be shipping at $299 like Meta’s latest smart glasses. Meta’s most premium offering, Oakley Meta Vanguard, retails for $499.

All of the upcoming Samsung Intelligent Eyewear models feature cameras on the front, although it’s possible Samsung will release camera-free glasses sometime in the future.

Even at a similar price, Samsung hopes its glasses will differentiate themselves from Meta’s offerings by being “an extension of the experience centered on the smartphone, rather than being a post-smartphone device.” Meta has been developing wearable computers for a while now, including VR and lighter XR headsets, often citing that they’re devices for the post-smartphone era. Samsung, instead, sees its glasses as a companion to phones, similar to smartwatches.

Samsung Intelligent Eyewear also has the advantage of having Gemini onboard and running Android XR, the official Google-built operating system for smart glasses and VR headsets. That means it’s sure to tie in with your Android-powered smartphone better than anything else on the market, something we’ve seen from Wear OS smartwatches.

Following a resurgence of 8GB RAM laptops earlier this year, and in the wake of promises to improve Windows 11 performance using just 8GB of RAM, Microsoft has today announced what it claims are a series of performance improvements. Driven by an ongoing global PC component shortage that is forcing manufacturers to dumb down specs, the company says that with 8GB of RAM, Windows is now 20% more responsive and 40% faster when it comes to multitasking.

The development shared today by Microsoft is an update to a commitment earlier this year to improve the quality and performance of Windows 11, a major bugbear of users since its launch. Microsoft says it has taken a three-pronged approach to memory optimization: making better use of memory in Windows 11 PCs, protecting interactions that need to feel instant, and ensuring key apps and Windows use less memory. While the company admits you'll be able to do more on 16GB or 32GB of RAM, it says "we're making sure you can do more, even with 8GB."

The headline performance gain is a claim that Windows is now up to 20% more responsive on 8GB PCs. Likewise, multitasking is now purportedly 40% faster in Microsoft's lab tests. Of course, these are internal tests conducted in favorable conditions by Microsoft.

Microsoft says it has tuned compression for useful apps and data, and can now keep up to 2GB more of your active data in memory, rather than moving it to storage. In practice, this should mean that apps and tabs left open should be less likely to reload when you go back to them.

The claim of 20% more responsiveness specifically relates to tasks like opening Start, searching, right-clicking, opening Settings, using the Snipping Tool, and opening File Explorer. The company says it has achieved this by backing off background tasks like indexing while you're using your PC actively. Edge now reportedly opens up to 33% faster. There's also an Efficiency Mode for Microsoft Teams, which can be set to on by default, improving launch times by 20%.

Microsoft says that its claims of 40% speed boosts to multitasking are based on a demanding workflow of 20 Microsoft Edge Tabs, a 4K video, large Word, PowerPoint, and Excel files, Outlook, and File Explorer all being opened one after the other.

Other improvements include reducing committed-memory growth by up to 900 MB in apps like Microsoft Edge and 365 apps, and reducing the memory footprint of Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook by 360MB. Third-party apps can also benefit from improved memory management, with Microsoft stating WhatsApp is already taking advantage.

Windows features and apps will share common parts, such as Search and Widgets using one web Engine, for instance. WinUI 3 apps like File Explorer and Notepad will be designed to use less memory and open faster, and Microsoft is working with PC makers and silicon manufacturers to reduce how much memory a PC needs to hold in reserve to support its hardware, making more space for Windows.
