#10259. The midterm elections’ biggest loser? Data centers

Data centers were on the ballot this election, and they lost.

While results from the midterm elections are still coming in, as of November 4, 38 out of 39 restrictions on data centers had passed—from temporary moratoriums on new construction to full bans. And multiple candidates who made opposition to data centers a key part of their campaign also won.

Take the example of William Lawrence, the Democratic candidate for the U.S. House of Representatives in Michigan’s purple 7th Congressional District, which Trump narrowly won in 2024. Lawrence, a progressive community organizer and cofounder of the Sunrise Movement, was new to politics and faced a challenge running against the Trump-backed incumbent, Tom Barrett. In the primary, facing two establishment Democrats who had raised more money, Lawrence won in part because he vowed to fight data centers.

“He found an issue that connected with local residents across partisanship,” says Matt Grossman, director of the Institute for Public Policy and Social Research at Michigan State University. Recent polls say that seven in 10 Americans don’t want data centers to be built in their communities, for reasons ranging from potential impacts on electric bills to noise and water use.

In his first ad, Lawrence stood at a farm and said, “Tech billionaires want to turn this field into a massive data center that’ll jack up our energy bills and ruin our home values.” After going to local planning meetings to watch data center developers pitch projects, he said that it was an “abuse of power” in communities that didn’t have the resources to fight back. He also called for other controls on technology, including a pause on development of advanced artificial intelligence and mandatory safety requirements for AI.  

Barrett, his Republican opponent, had supported data centers in the past. That included a vote for a version of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that would have stopped states’ ability to regulate AI, and likely also data centers, for a decade. (The provision was later taken out of the bill). The OBBBA includes tax breaks for companies building out AI infrastructure. Barrett also voted for the SPEED Act, which accelerates data center construction. As backlash to data centers grew, Barrett argued that communities should have local control over whether projects get built, but the message fell flat. Lawrence won.

Barrett was unpopular for other reasons—including the fact that he’d never held a local town hall—and it’s not clear that data centers were the thing that made voters push him out, versus anger about the Iran war, tariffs’ impact on the Michigan economy, and other factors. It’s probably too early to say that data centers as an issue swung a race, says Daniel Schiff, an associate professor of technology policy at Purdue University. But the election results affirm the opposition.

“If you had seen elections flip the other way, you would have said, oh, wow, this data center stuff actually isn’t that much of a concern for the public compared to other things,” Schiff says. That didn’t happen, and Democrats in other states who campaigned against data centers also won.

In Texas, Gina Hinojosa became first Democrat elected governor since 1990, beating the Republican incumbent Greg Abbott, after calling for a data center moratorium. (Abbott had called Texas the “epicenter of AI development,” before pivoting to pause new data centers; Hinojosa said she would go further.)

In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms, a Democrat, also won a race for governor after campaigning for a statewide moratorium on data centers. In New Mexico, the Democrat Deb Haaland pledged to implement a statewide moratorium and won the governor’s race. In Ohio, the Democrat Amy Acton called for a conditional moratorium and beat Vivek Ramaswamy in the governor’s race. Multiple candidates for Congress won on anti-data center platforms, like Sherrod Brown, who won a Senate seat after calling his Republican opponent the “face of data centers” in Ohio.

Opposition to data centers arguably was part of the reason that other races were much closer than expected—like in a race in southeast Georgia, where residents have opposed a new OpenAI data center. Trump won the district by nearly 50 points in the last presidential election, but the Republican candidate for Congress this year won by fewer than 3 points.

The question now is what public sentiment about data centers actually means for the tech industry’s plans for AI. It’s not clear that opposition to data centers is as much about AI as it is about issues like electricity prices and the climate impacts of soaring energy use. Those impacts aren’t baked in; it is possible to build data centers that run on clean energy paid for by tech companies, for example. But the skepticism about data centers is now so ingrained that it’s likely more moratoriums will pass.

That could mean that data center developers end up flocking to the few places left that might not fight them. “They’ll say, OK, we need to do this more quietly . . . we need to go to the communities that don’t speak back,” Schiff says. “That would be a plausible and unfortunate consequence.”

Tech companies are already struggling to access power for data centers, and as data centers themselves keep getting harder to build, it could also meaningfully slow down the spread of AI. Anthropic’s IPO filing said that the backlash against data centers could limit its ability to grow.

The tech industry has spent billions betting that it can build AI infrastructure fast enough to stay ahead of demand. But the midterms suggest that it may not be able to build fast enough to stay ahead of public opposition.

#10258. Meta paid billions, but largely escaped accountability for Cambridge Analytica. Here’s why

“The harm in this matter is difficult to overstate,” wrote a New Mexico judge who ordered tech giant Meta to pay one of the largest data privacy case penalties in American history. The $25 billion fine came in a case about how Trump campaign firm Cambridge Analytica deceptively used data from Facebook users without their permission to create psychographic profiles to target voters in the lead-up to the 2016 presidential election.

But the New Mexico penalty was for statements Facebook made that deceived users about data privacy and its response to Cambridge Analytica—not for the harm caused by how the harvested data was used. Those harms are alleged to include exploiting psychological vulnerabilities, targeting people’s fears and discouraging them from voting.

I’m a political communication scholar who studies propaganda, surveillance, and information warfare. My research helped expose the Cambridge Analytica scandal through U.K. newspaper The Guardian’s reporting on whistleblower accounts and the evidence I uncovered. That evidence was submitted to parliamentary and congressional investigations. I have followed the unfolding legal cases closely.

My takeaway from a decade of litigation is that Facebook has been penalized for misleading users and regulators about its data practices and its response to the Cambridge Analytica scandal. But I would contend that the company has largely escaped accountability for the underlying political exploitation of that data.

Investigative failures

The failure to bring cases around harms may be partly due to earlier failures to fully investigate the data misuse.

The Senate Intelligence Committee’s investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election encompassed Cambridge Analytica. However, the committee stated in its final report that it “was unable to obtain the corporate communications of Cambridge Analytica or its parent company SCL Group, which had already been seized by U.K. authorities.”

The relevant U.K. authorities, the Information Commissioner’s Office, which governs data protection and took possession of Cambridge Analytica’s servers, told me in response to my 2021 Freedom of Information Act request that the Senate committee staff made initial inquiries to the office but appear not to have followed up with a formal request, “so no information sharing has taken place.” Without a formal request, the Senate Intelligence Committee’s investigation lacked important data.

At the same time, the U.K. investigations of Cambridge Analytica’s use of personal data to manipulate voting behavior focused on the referendum of British voters over whether to leave the EU, not events in the U.S.

Facebook user data was at the heart of the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

A 2020 documentary film I advised as a researcher, People You May Know, raised questions about Cambridge Analytica’s work with an app marketed to American churches, called Gloo, that used Cambridge Analytica’s Facebook data-derived psychographic profiling in their communities. Evidence in the New Mexico case reinvigorates these questions about the full extent of the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

The judge in the case ruled Facebook knew that its own processes for investigating whether apps misused personal data were inadequate and that it could not enforce deletion of the data. The judge also concluded the company failed to notify users about thousands of applications associated with data misuse. Meta said it would appeal the decision.

Meta responded to a request for comment with the company’s official statement about the New Mexico ruling, arguing the case “seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online.” Meta did not address the issue of its own role in the data privacy violations committed by Cambridge Analytica.

Escaping further scrutiny

Meta is also trying to close the door on further claims before they are litigated.

In August 2026, on the eve of a child-safety trial in federal court in Oakland, California, Meta settled with a bipartisan coalition of state attorneys general for roughly $17 billion. The agreement includes 47 states, the District of Columbia, and two U.S. territories. Folded into that deal was an allocation of $459.3 million to settle Cambridge Analytica-related claims held by participating states.

The participating attorneys general agreed, to the extent of their authority, to “fully, finally, and forever” release Meta from “any and all Claims, whether known or unknown, whether accrued or unaccrued.” By expressly encompassing “unknown” and “unaccrued” claims, the agreement reached beyond what investigators had already uncovered. Participating states accepted payment to give up claims arising from Meta’s conduct even if they did not yet know those claims existed.

A decade-old matter—Facebook’s role in the Cambridge Analytica scandal—was quietly brushed under the rug in an unrelated lawsuit about harm to teens.

From the 2019 Federal Trade Commission order to the 2022 class action settlement to August 2026’s multistate deal, settlements and releases have meant the company paid a relatively small price for its deception while not having the harms from the data exploitation adjudicated. Ultimately, the biggest privacy judgment in American history stands as a measure of the cover-up, not the alleged crime.

Other scholars and I regularly call attention to the lack of comprehensive U.S. privacy legislation, but there remain other legal pathways to pursue the harms Cambridge Analytica wrought. States like New Mexico can continue the fight, and Attorney General Raúl Torrez, who brought the case, promised, “We’re just getting started.”

Dissenting from the FTC’s 2019 settlement, then-Commissioner Rohit Chopra criticized the failure to consider “Facebook’s unjust enrichment.” He said “the company’s potential exposure is likely far greater” than the $5 billion imposed by the FTC settlement.

What price for the harm?

The question remains what exactly Facebook gained from enabling Cambridge Analytica’s abuses. Authorities could also investigate harmful data use for any other apps Facebook may have failed to fully assess, including any associated with Cambridge Analytica’s projects.

If the deception about Cambridge Analytica is worth $25 billion, I believe the public is entitled to know what the underlying harms to them are worth. New Mexico opted out of the 2026 multistate settlement and proved that a state willing to go to trial against Meta can win.

The next task, in my view, is to investigate fully and, where legal claims remain available, pursue accountability for harms resulting from the data exploitation. Otherwise, Cambridge Analytica will remain at the heart of the most consequential privacy scandal in American history, whose full harms have not been tested in court.

Emma L. Briant is a visiting associate professor at the Lucy Family Institute for Data and Society at the University of Notre Dame.

#10257. The Hidden Problems Behind Website-to-CRM Integrations (and How to Prevent Them)

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Connecting a website form to a customer relationship management (CRM) system may seem straightforward. A developer collects information from a form, sends it to an API endpoint, and checks whether a new contact appears in the CRM.

The integration may work perfectly during the first test. However, problems can appear after the website goes live. Some leads may not reach the CRM, duplicate contacts may appear, or important customer information may be missing.

These issues are not always easy to notice. A visitor might see a confirmation message even when the CRM has failed to save their information.

This guide explains common problems in website-to-CRM integrations and practical ways developers can prevent them.

A website-to-CRM integration allows information collected through a website to move into a CRM system. This usually happens through an API or webhook.

For example, when someone completes a contact form, the website collects their name, email address, phone number, and other details. The integration then sends this information to the CRM, where it can be stored and used by the relevant team.

An API integration provides a structured way for two applications to exchange information. Developers who need additional background can also read OpenHerald's overview of API integration.

The process usually involves several steps:

The website validates the submitted information.

The application sends a request to the CRM.

The CRM checks the request and processes the data.

The website or backend handles the response.

Each step needs to work correctly. If one part fails, the information may not reach its destination.

One important rule is to avoid displaying a successful submission message before the application has safely accepted and stored the data.

Data issues are among the most frequent problems in website-to-CRM integrations. They may not appear during development because test submissions usually contain simple, predictable information.

Real visitors enter data in different formats and may submit the same form more than once.

A visitor might complete a contact form and later download a resource using the same email address. If the integration creates a new CRM record every time, the same person may appear several times.

To prevent this, developers should decide how existing contacts will be identified.

Email addresses are commonly used for matching. Before comparing them, the application should remove unnecessary spaces and convert the address to a consistent format.

These values should be treated consistently.

Where supported, an upsert operation can create a new contact or update an existing one instead of creating unnecessary duplicates.

Website forms and CRM systems do not always use the same field structure.

A website may collect a visitor's full name in one field, while the CRM expects separate first-name and last-name values. Other fields may have different names or requirements.

Developers should create a clear mapping between website fields and CRM fields before building the integration.

They should also check which fields are required. If the CRM requires information that the website does not collect, the request may fail.

Different systems may store information in different formats.

For example, one application might use United Kingdom, while another expects UK. Dates, phone numbers, and country values can also create problems.

A reliable integration should validate and standardise these values before sending them to the CRM.

A contact record is more useful when the sales or marketing team knows where the visitor came from.

However, integrations sometimes send only basic contact information and leave out details such as campaign source, landing page, and referral information.

Developers should identify which tracking fields are useful and include them in the integration where appropriate.

Even an integration that works correctly at launch can stop working later.

Authentication credentials may expire, permissions may change, or an API provider may limit the number of requests an application can make.

Three areas deserve particular attention.

Many APIs use access tokens or other credentials to verify requests. Some tokens expire and must be refreshed.

If an application does not handle token renewal correctly, requests may begin failing without an obvious problem on the website.

Developers should implement the authentication process recommended by the CRM provider and monitor failed requests.

An API provider may restrict the number of requests allowed within a particular period.

A marketing campaign can suddenly increase website traffic and generate more form submissions than usual. If the integration exceeds the provider's limit, some requests may be rejected.

The application should recognise rate-limit responses and retry requests according to the provider's instructions.

An integration should not receive more access than it needs.

For example, a form submission service may only need permission to create or update contacts. Giving it full administrative access increases unnecessary security risks.

Use the minimum permissions required for the integration to function.

External services can experience outages, network delays, and temporary errors. If the website sends a form submission directly to the CRM without storing it first, a failed request could mean a lost lead.

A safer approach is to separate receiving a submission from delivering it to the CRM.

Validate the form information on the server.

Store the submission safely in your own system.

Send it to the CRM through a background process.

Retry temporary failures after an appropriate delay.

Flag permanent failures for manual review.

This approach gives the application another opportunity to deliver information when the CRM becomes available again.

A request might reach the CRM successfully, but the response could be lost because of a network problem. The website may then retry the same request, creating a duplicate contact.

Idempotency helps prevent this situation. The application can use a stable identifier for each submission so that repeating the same operation does not create another record.

For example, a combination of the form ID and a normalised email address may help identify repeated submissions. The exact approach depends on the CRM's API capabilities.

This is an illustrative example. Functions such as crmUpsertContact() and scheduleRetry() need to be implemented according to the application and CRM being used.

The important point is that every submission should have a known status: successfully delivered, waiting for another attempt, or requiring manual attention.

A working integration should also protect the quality and security of the information it collects.

Public forms can receive automated submissions from bots. Without appropriate protection, these entries can fill the CRM with unwanted records.

Validation should happen on the server, even if the website already checks information in the browser.

Some forms collect permission to send marketing communications.

If a visitor selects a consent checkbox, that information should also be passed to the CRM. Otherwise, the CRM may contain the contact details without a reliable record of the visitor's choice.

Where relevant, store the consent value, the wording or version displayed, and the time the visitor gave consent.

An integration should only send the information needed for its intended purpose.

Collecting unnecessary personal details increases the amount of information the application must protect and maintain.

Developers should also understand where submitted information is stored, including databases, queues, application logs, and the CRM.

Testing an integration before launch is important, but monitoring it afterwards is just as necessary.

A successful test does not prove that every future submission will work.

The following checks can help identify problems early.

Compare the number of website form submissions with the number of contacts successfully created or updated in the CRM.

A growing difference between the two numbers may indicate that some requests are failing.

Application logs should record the reason a request failed and include a submission identifier where possible.

Avoid storing complete personal details in logs unless there is a specific, justified need.

Developers should configure notifications when the integration's failure rate exceeds an acceptable threshold.

This makes it easier to investigate problems before they affect a large number of submissions.

A scheduled test submission can help confirm that the complete process is still working.

For example, a test lead can be sent periodically and checked to confirm that it reaches the CRM correctly.

Someone should be responsible for monitoring the integration.

This person or team should review errors, check API changes, monitor credentials, and investigate changes to CRM fields.

Without a clear owner, small problems can remain unnoticed for a long time.

Documentation makes integrations easier to maintain and troubleshoot.

It does not need to be complicated. A short reference document covering the main rules can save considerable time when another developer needs to work on the system.

Before deployment, developers should also test unusual situations.

Testing these situations helps reveal weaknesses that ordinary form submissions may not expose.

What is the most common website-to-CRM integration problem?

Duplicate contacts and incorrect field mapping are common problems. They usually happen when the website and CRM handle data differently.

How can developers prevent duplicate contacts?

Normalise email addresses, use a consistent matching rule, and use an upsert operation or idempotency mechanism where the CRM supports it.

Should a website send form data directly to a CRM?

For more reliable handling, the application should first validate and safely store the submission. A background process can then deliver it to the CRM and retry temporary failures.

How can I tell if a CRM integration has stopped working?

Compare website submission counts with CRM records, monitor failed requests, and schedule regular test submissions.

Who should be responsible for maintaining the integration?

Assign a developer or technical team to monitor the connection, review errors, maintain credentials, and respond to API changes.

Developers can make these integrations more reliable by validating information on the server, storing submissions before delivery, using safe retry mechanisms, and monitoring the results after launch.

The goal is simple: every valid submission should reach the CRM, and every failed submission should be visible and recoverable rather than silently lost.

#10256. Gemini 4 Carbon lags just behind Claude in benchmark, but wins in value

Google’s new frontier model, Gemini 4 Carbon, brings some welcome improvements and while it doesn’t top the charts in a new benchmark, it does provide much more bang for your buck.

SemiAnalysis, an AI research and analysis firm, recently published its new frontier-level benchmark, GDPx which includes numbers for Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon model. The leaderboard includes every major frontier model from the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta and details both the score and cost for each model.

The benchmark includes 206 tasks across finance, materials science, cybersecurity, software engineering, legal, biology, and several other domains (topics).

Topping the results is Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5, but Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon is very close behind. The difference between the two is relatively minimal, but the cost is the biggest factor to consider here. Where Claude’s cost came out to around $51 per task, Gemini was just over $16 per task. Gemini also beat the next model on the list, GPT-6 Astra, which scored lower while costing more than both at about $54 per task.

The report notes that taking out cybersecurity, biology, and alignment domains shuffles the results. Safety guardrails in Claude and GPT models puts GPT-6 Astra at the top of the list with GPT 6.1 Sol and Claude Sonnet 5.5 outranking Gemini 4 Carbon. SemiAnalysis says that this better aligns with their “subjective impressions” of each model.

As for Google’s existing frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, it ranks in eighth place on both lists, beating Meta’s Muse Wonder, but below Wonder Full. Argon’s costs in this particular benchmark are only slightly lower than Carbon.

Both of Google’s models score better than OpenAI and Anthropic models when focused on cybersecurity, but do fall behind Meta’s Muse models, which the benchmark found to be the best “by a meaningful margin.”

Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon on October 28 and touted “significant gains,” but the public release date has not been confirmed just yet. It is “coming soon” for most customers. Google’s own benchmark, below, beat GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5 in many aspects.

#10255. IBM and UC Berkeley Diagnose Why Enterprise Agents Fail Using IT-Bench and MAST

Ayhan Sebin Saurabh Jha Rohan Arora Daby Sow Mert Cemri Melissa Pan Ion Stoica

ITBench HF Space ITBench HF Dataset MAST HF Dataset ITBench Github MAST Github

IBM Research and UC Berkeley collaborated to study how agentic LLM systems break in real-world IT automation, for tasks involving incident triage, logs/metrics queries, and Kubernetes actions in long-horizon tool loops.

Benchmarks typically reduce performance to a single number, telling you whether an agent failed but never why. To solve this black-box problem, we applied MAST (Multi-Agent System Failure Taxonomy), an emerging practice for diagnosing agentic reliability ). By leveraging MAST to analyze ITBench—the industry benchmark for SRE, Security, and FinOps automation—we turned raw execution traces into structured failure signatures, revealing exactly what broke and how to fix it. We annotated 310 ITBench SRE traces across three distinct model classes: Gemini-3-Flash, Kimi-K2, and GPT-OSS-120B.

Takeaways from our analysis when building agents:

If you’re building agents for enterprise IT workflows, this is the kind of evaluation you want: not just “did it pass?”, but “what broke, where, and what intervention is most leverageable?”

Benchmarks like ITBench are becoming the standard for measuring agentic performance in high-stakes IT automation tasks. In ITBench, agents act as Site Reliability Engineers (SREs) or Security Analysts tasked with diagnosing Kubernetes outages, patching vulnerabilities, or managing cloud costs in production environments.

This benchmarks use success rate as a main metric to evaluate agents. However, this metric is insufficient for engineering robust systems. Knowing that an agentic system achieves a 14% success rate on ITBench tells us that it failed, but not why: Did it fail because it forgot the context? Because it hallucinated a command? Or because it simply did not terminate?

Without a comprehensive approach to diagnose these failures, developers are left guessing, often resorting to blind prompting tweaks that solve one problem only to create another.

As a new standard to analyze the failure modes of complex agentic systems, we developed MAST (Multi-Agent System Failure Taxonomy). MAST brings more insights and open up the opaque evaluation of these benchmarks. Derived from a rigorous analysis of over 1,600 traces across seven different frameworks, MAST provides a standardized taxonomy for agent failures.

MAST converts unstructured execution logs into structured "failure vectors" based on 14 distinct patterns across three key categories:

We stress-test the idea of using MAST to make agent evaluations actionable and gain insights on the failure modes by applying it to ITBench, a popular evaluation suite for IT automation tasks across SRE, Security/Compliance, and FinOps.

We annotated 310 ITBench SRE execution traces produced by an SRE agent built with Codex in realistic environments. These traces capture natural language interactions between agents and their tools across three models representing different capability tiers: Gemini-3-Flash, Kimi-K2, and GPT-OSS-120B. This lets us look past simple success metrics and investigate the distinct failure signatures driving these results. For this we use the recall scores, as the models by design only output a maximum of 3-5 outputs and SREs prefer the recall scores over F-1 score.

Below, we detail the findings from this diagnostic analysis.

When we examine the failed traces, a clear hierarchy of complexity becomes apparent across the three models. This is measured by the number of distinct failure modes observed per failed run.

This disparity in failure mode density reveals a fundamental difference in how these systems break down. Gemini-3-Flash exhibits a surgical failure profile. Even in unsuccessful runs, it maintains high internal coherence and typically fails due to a single isolated failure, such as an incorrect verification step. These failures are precise and far easier to diagnose.

On the opposite end of the spectrum, GPT-OSS-120B suffers from cascading collapse. In these traces, we observe that errors tend to compound over time. A small reasoning mismatch early in the process often leads to a deviation from the task specification, which in turn triggers a total derailment of the agent. Kimi-K2 represents the middle ground, where failures are more frequent and complex than the frontier model but do not reach the systemic instability seen in the 120B open weights model.

The significance of this finding is that a higher success rate is often accompanied by isolated failure. Systems that fail with fewer simultaneous problems are far more predictable and simpler to improve through targeted engineering interventions.

Perhaps the most critical insight from MAST is distinguishing between failures that the system can tolerate versus those that are fatal to success of the downstream task. By comparing the distribution of failure modes in Successful Traces vs. Failed Traces, we can classify them into three categories.

Across all three models, certain failure modes appear frequently even in runs that ultimately succeed. These are often structural frictions rather than terminal bugs.

This separation is where MAST proves its value. It allows us to ignore the bening failures like repetition that often occurs in troubleshooting, and focus instead on fatal failures that killed a run.

Certain behaviors strongly separate success from failure. When these modes appear, the probability of a successful outcome drops precipitously. The most prominent example is FM-3.3 (Incorrect Verification). This mode shows a 52 percent increase in failed Gemini-3-Flash traces compared to its successful ones. Other prominent failure modes are 1.5 (Unaware of Termination Conditions) and 2.6 (Reasoning Action Mismatch).

If these happen, the run is likely dead; guiding practitioners to develop robust context management strategies across agents in the system and multiple turns of interactions.

Gemini-3-Flash is highly efficient, but its primary bottleneck is its tendency to assume success without rigorous proof. Its failure signature is dominated by a massive delta in verification errors. It often identifies the correct signals but terminates before cross-referencing them against the ground truth. To fix this, developers should implement an external verification gate. By requiring tool-based evidence like a cleared alert or a healthy metric threshold before allowing the agent to exit, we can mitigate this model’s inherent overconfidence.

While termination confusion (FM-3.1 and FM-1.5) is the prevalent failure mode for Kimi-K2, its failed trajectories are defined by a pervasive Action-Reasoning Mismatch (FM-2.6), which is present in a staggering 92% of its failures.

Kimi-K2 is a good example of an overthinking model, its reasoning chains are often too long but can fail at execution.

GPT-OSS-120B exhibits the most unstable failure signature of the cohort. This model exhibits an average of 5.3 distinct failure modes per failed trace, indicating a fundamental inability to maintain internal state.

In summary, MAST lets you split failure modes into two buckets:

These are failures which are not fatal and from which the system can recover to successfully complete the task.

These are failures from which the system typically cannot recover.

This is the “richer understanding” piece: two models can have the same success rate on a small slice, yet fail for entirely different reasons—requiring different fixes.

MAST is a tool that inspects the agentic system traces to identify fine-grain failure types that support system development and debugging. In this blog, we show that by applying MAST to ITBench, we move from generic observations ("Open models struggle") to a concrete engineering roadmap that help improving the performance of agentic systems relying on thse models, e.g.:

Develop and run interactive code notebooks with JupyterLab

#10254. Gen Z is souring on dating apps. This very NSFW one is booming

Connie Collins, a 25-year-old sex educator, walked through the unlocked door of a stylish apartment in Williamsburg, Brooklyn, to find a man lying naked and face down on a bed. “I put on a strap and just started strapping away at him,” she says. “It was just super crazy. I’ve never done anything like that before.”

The pair didn’t know each other’s names, nor had they seen each other’s faces. Though they’d later develop a brief friendship, they had met only hours earlier, under pseudonyms, on an app named Pure, billed as “the open-minded dating app.”

Even as mainstream dating apps scramble to respond to dwindling subscribers and Gen Z skepticism, 12-year-old Pure—which presents itself as an alternative to traditional services like Hinge and Tinder, and as an even less inhibited version of kink-friendly Feeld—has been on a tear. In February, the company reported that it had reached $100 million in annual revenue. Pure tells Fast Company that it has now reached . . .

a $220 million run rate—and is forecasting to double that figure next year. Over the past year, Pure’s revenue has more than doubled in the U.S, its biggest market. 

The sex-forward dating app is free to download but men and nonbinary users must pay for a subscription ($13.99 a week, $648 a year) to initiate chats and maximize their visibility. Women have access to most features on the app for free, though the Pure Queens subscription (starting at $4.99 a week) gives them access to more controls. Pure says that its users are split 60-40 between men and women—and most are Gen Z and millennial. (Tinder, which appeals to the same demographic, has a ratio of roughly 75% male, 25% female.)

“People are getting a bit tired of all the traditional swipe-based dating apps and they’re looking for something different,” says Pure’s CEO, Luka Dremelj. He credits Pure’s success to its unique interface and user experience. Users on Pure don’t swipe through profiles, accepting and rejecting matches. Instead, they scroll through a feed of “personal ads” posted by other users, expressing interests, desires, or provocative come-ons. That feed is full of individuals who have identified similar turn-ons—everything from music and massage to one-night stands, foot fetishes, and dominant and submissive relationships. 

Though it facilitates in-person connections, Pure is just as much about chatting and sexting, allowing users to share explicit photos and videos, which disappear after viewing, and engage in video calls. As dating apps contend with Gen Z users who are either uninterested or too anxious to meet in person, Pure offers a different proposition: allowing them to explore their sexuality behind a screen, with limited human contact. 

The app’s unorthodox approach to privacy—all users are anonymous, even to the app itself, which doesn’t verify identity—is one of its biggest draws, reducing barriers to connections and letting people explore their turn-ons without inhibition. But, as a recent lawsuit in Texas indicates, it may leave some users exposed. 

A new design language

Pure’s approachability starts with its design language, which is filled with bright colors and playful, hand-drawn illustrations after a redesign earlier this year. “We’re bringing this human touch to the user experience,” says Dremelj, who joined the company in 2022, shortly after RM Equity Partners, a European private equity firm, bought the app. “There’s a bit of humor in there.”

Users first experience this humor during the onboarding process. They begin by choosing their gender and sexuality on screens that feature whimsical drawings. Then they create their “ad,” which serves almost like an old-school newspaper personal, enticing people to click on their profile, which can be customized with photos and different background colors and designs. 

To make it easier for users to share their desires, Pure allows them to select from a list of more than 20 turn-ons to display on their profiles—each portrayed by illustrated icons. Those options include feminism (tagline: “let’s dismantle the patriarchy together”), outdoor hangs (“fresh air, dirty thoughts”), home video (illustrated by a clapperboard with “take 69” on it), and therapy (“mindful of my relationship with myself and others”). Others are kinkier and include edging, cuckolding, and wax play.

Users’ turn-ons are also displayed on their personal ads, which include a brief tagline stating what they’re looking for and optional photos. Users discover one another’s ads in a feed that Pure can adjust. “Sometimes, instead of leading with photos, we will put someone’s turn-ons as the first thing users might read about them in the feed,” Dremelj says. When two users express the same desires, the app might inform them that they have mutual turn-ons to give them a conversation starter. 

Crucially, users can always go back and look at profiles they may have initially passed on. There’s no such thing as a “hard pass” in the open world of Pure. 

Private parts

While Pure’s visual design sets it apart from other apps, its approach to privacy shapes virtually every interaction. An app designed for casual encounters and sexting has to walk a thin line between offering users anonymity while keeping them safe. 

To start, every user is assigned a random username, though they can use their real name if they choose. They’re not required to share any pictures or answer any prompts about themselves. 

Most dating and hook-up apps take an à la carte approach to privacy. A user might fill in their profile, then toggle over to settings to make sure that location services, or features that detect mutual friends, are turned off. By contrast, Pure’s settings default to anonymity. “The traditional discourse around sharing information on dating apps is that we have to make the online world smaller, more controlled, and less anonymous,” says Sergej Vujanović, Pure’s chief product officer. “I feel that some level of anonymity at the start is great, and then you can decide on your terms when you want to share. We’re not prohibiting sharing more.”

Dilara Doshi, a Berlin-based, 31-year-old content creator, joined Pure two years ago to explore her sexuality. She says that she usually meets up with someone within hours of beginning a chat on the app. “I display pictures of my face. I have a picture in a bikini, so you can see my body shape,” she says. “I use my real name and my real age. Some other users actually hide their faces on their profiles with a cap, or put an emoji on top, or sunglasses, or they write, ‘Hey, if it’s a vibe, I can send you pictures of me.’”

All content from Pure chats disappears after 24 hours, though both users can agree to remove the time limit. Photos and videos also disappear after 24 hours, and can be opened only once. 

“Sometimes people ask to move the conversation to WhatsApp, but I don’t usually say yes to that because it’s sexting,” Doshi says. “I like that our communication disappears on Pure. I don’t want footage being saved.” (Grindr provides some comparable safeguards, including self-destructing imagery alongside settings that allow members to obscure their physical distance and opt out of appearing in local discovery feeds.)

Screenshots are also banned on Pure, and if a user tries to take one, the other party is notified. When she started using the app, Collins attempted to take a screenshot of a conversation to send to her friends. When the app informed the person she was chatting with, Collins was embarrassed but also relieved: “Knowing that I, a well-intentioned person, tried to screenshot a conversation and couldn’t, made me feel really safe.”

Someone could still use a separate device to photograph whatever is on the phone, as Aaron Rose, a cybersecurity expert at Check Point Software Technologies, points out. He also notes, “Without identity verification, you don’t necessarily know offhand that who you’re talking to is an actual human being. It could be a bot.” 

Pure encourages users to keep all their interactions within the app until they meet up in person. “When you get into a chat with somebody, if you share a social handle with them, we’ll send you a notification asking, Hey, are you sure you want to share that? Because then the other party can usually identify you,” says Vujanović, the chief product officer.

Before meeting up with another user, Collins will often video chat with them within the app to make sure they’re representing themselves accurately. “I did it with somebody recently,” she says. “We got to have a preliminary conversation about what we would want if we were together.”

Doshi uses the app in her native Turkey, where many users are anonymous to protect themselves. But anonymity can be a double-edged sword. “Because I talk openly about sex, sometimes I have hateful comments from Turkish men on social media and on the app,” she says. “When I see a Turkish man matching me and he wants to meet me, I’m like maybe he’s very conservative, and maybe it’s just a trap. Sometimes gay men or young women get catfished on [dating and relationship platforms], and then something happens to them.”

The risks of prioritizing anonymity 

Pure doesn’t require photo or video verification for users nor does it have an age verification process, except in regions where local laws mandate such proof, like the U.K. “We believe the best thing would be that the verification process would be done already at the level of Apple and Google in their app stores,” Vujanović says. “The app is built around privacy, so when you ask users to upload their ID, they’re sometimes feeling a bit reluctant.” 

This approach sets it apart from Tinder, which introduced Face Check for all new users in every territory last year. The tool doesn’t ask for a government ID, but does compel all new users to go through a video selfie verification process. Match Group, Tinder’s owner, told Congressional investigators that pilots of the tool reduced user interactions with scam accounts by 70% in the U.S.

Pure offers a similar feature, but it’s not required for users. Once a user is approved, a verification badge is displayed on their profile. Pure also has a feature called True Photos, which verifies photos taken in the app at a particular moment. Users can request a True Photo from someone while chatting; a photo will then appear with a verification checkmark proving that it was taken recently within the app. A feature called Safety Signal also lets a user share their last known location and their date’s Pure profile photos with a trusted person through a password-protected link.

Still, the lack of identity and age verification introduces risks, and makes it difficult for the app to police bad actors. A lawsuit filed in Harris County, Texas, in October alleges that, in March, a 35-year-old former police officer posed as a 16-year-old on Pure, where he connected with and arranged to meet a 13-year-old. The suit says he brought her to his home, gave her drugs, and sexually assaulted her. 

The company says it has yet to be contacted by U.S. law enforcement and learned of the incident through an article in the Houston Chronicle. “We are waiting for either law enforcement or the lawyers of the plaintiff to get back to us and tell us the details so that we can actually just check what happened,” Vujanović says. Pure adds that until it hears more, it can’t verify that either individual was ever on the app.

Something for everyone

I joined Pure while reporting this article, uploading three pictures of myself, including my reporter headshot. I also clearly designated in my bio that I was a journalist looking to learn more about the app. 

Within an hour, I had more than 500 likes. When I matched with other users to ask them questions, I was often greeted with an ephemeral picture. I made the mistake of opening a few; they were all dick pics.

My experience is common for many women on the app. Doshi tells me that sometimes the volume of interest on the app can be overwhelming. Upon joining, she received 900 likes in a day, compared to 40 on Hinge. 

Collins says that the app has been validating for her as a queer woman of color. “I’ve never had these many matches before in my life. It felt like I was being shown to any and everyone, and my profile didn’t feel so thrown at the bottom of the pile,” she says.

She pays for a Pure Queens subscription, which she considers worthwhile for customizable filters that let her set her match radius and age range. She dislikes some subscriber perks other users pay extra for, like the one that gives them direct access to her inbox without matching with her first. She values the block feature.

Vujanović says that the app has tested AI-driven features that help users choose appealing pictures and help them fill out their bio (features available on Match Group apps and Bumble). The initiatives were nixed when they didn’t increase user interactions or connections. What does help with connections on Pure: when people use their anonymity to frankly describe their turn-ons in hope that someone will share them. 

Sometimes they strike out. When a user messaged me asking if I enjoyed the idea of multiple male partners peeing on me, I responded no. I added that I wasn’t on the platform to discuss such things.

But perhaps someone else was out there. “People have very, very, very specific kinks,” Doshi notes. “I hope they get lucky on Pure because I imagine it’s hard to find people who share them.” One thing she is clear on: “I don’t think AI can help so much.”

The engine drives a 400v motor-generator that electrically drives the propellers.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Researchers at U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command (DEVCOM) Army Research Laboratory (ARL) recently successfully flew the VICTOR hybrid electric drone with a heavy-fuel rotary engine, rapidly developed thanks to metal 3D printing — allowing the drone to extract more performance out of the denser but less volatile military fuel source.

The heavy fuel (JP8) used in the drone is a denser kerosene-based fuel source compared to regular jet fuel, making it desirable to reduce total fuel load or increase mileage. The JP8 fuel is part of the military’s initiative to power as much of its gas equipment on a single fuel source. However, JP8 is less volatile and harder to atomize, making it a challenge to achieve peak efficiency. Furthermore, the fuel’s flash point is 140℉, compared to gasoline’s -40℉, requiring the engine to have a much higher compression to ignite it, making pressure leaks a common issue.

JP-8 fuel on aircraft and drones is not uncommon; however, the ARL researchers wanted to further optimize the heavy-fuel rotary engine to extract more performance and improve its design. The researchers used computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and a clean-sheet design (designing from scratch, essentially), allowing the engineers to come up with more innovative solutions to get more out of the engine with less.

"The use of advanced manufacturing, including 3D metal printing, allowed us to rapidly redesign engine components based on lessons learned through experimentation,” Dr. Kweon, one of the ARL researchers, said to Army.mil. Dr. Kweon further explained that 3D printing allowed them to design an air-cooled engine and ditch a bulky liquid cooling system, reducing the size of the propulsion system. The rapid iteration eventually allowed the researchers to improve fuel atomization and decrease compression leaks.

The heavy-fuel rotary engine doesn’t actually drive the drone’s propellers directly; it uses the engine to spin a 400-volt motor-generator to generate electricity to drive the propeller motors, allowing the engine to spin independently at its most optimal RPM — similar to some hybrid EVs on the road today, except that the engine doesn’t have a mechanical link to the propellers. This system may include a battery for the drone to fly without the engine running; however, the US military has not disclosed much about the VICTOR drone’s battery configuration.

The VICTOR drone is a vertical take-off and landing (VTOL) unmanned aircraft, able to fly without a runway. The US Army has shared a video of its first flight, and the drone is able to land and take off in terrain that would otherwise be impossible for other non-VTOL two-winged aircraft. With a battery system, the drone could cover large distances on a single fuel-up, and air-cooling gives it another layer of robustness, avoiding maintenance on a liquid cooling system.

#10252. From postpartum to menopause, ‘brain fog’ affects women at work. Here’s how leaders can help

I was four centimeters dilated and in active labor with my first child when I successfully pitched our startup’s $5 million seed round. Two years later, I closed our $10 million Series A just seven days after giving birth to my second child.

These are the kinds of stories about ambitious women that we love to celebrate. The startup founder who pumps in the airport bathroom on her way to a client meeting (been there). The seasoned executive who barely misses a beat through perimenopausal brain fog and hot flashes. The new mom who’s back to work just a few weeks after giving birth, stitches burning and breasts leaking (been there, too).

I’m proud of what I’ve accomplished, and I’m in awe of the women out there doing it all—and doing it well. But I have begun to wonder what exactly we are celebrating when we tell these stories, and whether there might be a bit of patriarchy hiding in the applause.

Because while I was navigating some of the most consequential moments of my professional life, I was also experiencing a level of mental, physical, and emotional vulnerability that was entirely new to me.

Under pressure

I have always been someone who can handle pressure. Stressful jobs are nothing new to me. And running a startup means confronting high-stakes situations and ambiguity daily. Usually, I address it, solve it, and move on.

When I was pregnant and postpartum, I was still able to do all of those things, but my experience of doing them had changed. Situations I would normally navigate without a hitch felt higher-stakes and took a greater mental toll. Problems I knew perfectly well how to solve felt emotionally consuming.  

For centuries, women’s biology was used as evidence that we were inferior to men and incapable of doing the jobs men do. We’re “too emotional,” “too hormonal,” “too distracted by birthing and raising children.” These traits, the story went, made women unsuitable for positions of consequence and authority requiring sound judgment.  

Women have spent the past decades fighting that narrative and have made progress. 

However, we have fought so hard to prove that our biology doesn’t make us less competent that we’ve ended up feeling like we have to pretend it doesn’t affect us at all.

The menopause factor

This is just as relevant for the 50 million women navigating perimenopause, many at the height of their careers. Two-thirds of women in menopause report reduced work performance associated with menopausal symptoms. And another recent study found that 66% of women felt their coworkers and managers didn’t understand what they were going through.

It’s not hard to understand why women might hesitate to speak openly about our experiences. When we’ve fought so hard to prove that our biology doesn’t hamper our competence, acknowledging that it affects us at all can feel like failure.

And when we celebrate women for performing at a high level through pregnancy, postpartum, and perimenopause as though those biological transitions don’t affect us, we reinforce that narrative.

Assimilation not liberation

That is not liberation. That’s assimilation to a corporate world built for a worker who is unaffected by reproduction, changing biology, and hormonal transitions. We’ve fought so hard for a seat at the table, only to find that seat is contingent on our bodies performing exactly like men’s.

In our current hustle culture, women have two choices. We can be honest about how our biology is affecting us—talk openly about the brain fog, the emotional vulnerability, the sleep deprivation, the anxiety, the physical suffering—and risk being perceived as incompetent, unstable, and unfit to make important decisions or lead teams. Or, we can conceal the realities of pregnancy, postpartum, and perimenopause, perform our way through them, and then receive applause for proving they don’t affect our performance. 

Neither feels much like progress. Either way, we are still treating the reality of being a woman as  something to overcome. 

What leaders can do 

As a CEO, I firmly believe that we won’t solve this with another benefits program or a well-intentioned webinar about “women’s health and wellness.” It requires more open dialogue with employees, including being vulnerable about your own lived experiences. 

Stop celebrating invulnerability. When we celebrate women who do incredible things while pregnant, postpartum, or perimenopausal, it raises the question: Are we applauding their achievements, or their willingness to deprioritize their well-being and recovery?  

As leaders, we shape workplace culture through what we reward and recognize. We must applaud women’s performance without compelling them to make their physical and emotional realities invisible.

Normalize it. One of the most powerful things leaders can do is talk honestly about how pregnancy, postpartum, and perimenopause can affect how we feel and function without diminishing our professional competence. 

When leaders speak openly about their own experiences and vulnerabilities, they enable others to do the same. A CEO who acknowledges that she’s dealing with pregnancy brain or postpartum anxiety while continuing to lead effectively demonstrates that these experiences are not incompatible with doing her job well. 

Build support into your workplace. Create flexible structures that allow women to adjust to and nurture their biological realities, such as returning to work part-time, giving them control over their return-to-work plans, making it normal to ask a colleague to cover a meeting, or structuring the days around when they feel they can work their best. The point isn’t to lower our expectations, but rather to give talented women the conditions they need to meet them, without requiring them to prove how much they can endure.

We have spent generations proving that women can succeed in a world designed without their biology in mind. It’s time to build a world where they no longer have to.

#10250. Playful wants the masses to start vibe coding

Mike Harrington and Darrin Massena think that making an app with AI is still too hard.

While you can ask Claude or ChatGPT to build something for you, that demands at least some awareness of programming frameworks and hosting options. AI app builders like Replit and Cursor also aim to be professional-grade development tools for businesses, not something you’d use to quickly scratch a personal itch.

Harrington’s and Messena’s startup, Playful, wants to bring vibe coding to a much broader audience. With a handful of simple prompts, Playful will build web-based apps and games that you can push to your phone and share with friends. Users can create up to two apps for free and use them for up to 30 days, at which point the service requires a $10 per month subscription.

“It’s for an audience that is less technical, for an audience that until recently didn’t even understand that they could make apps,” Harrington says.

Playful isn’t the first company to try bringing AI app creation to mainstream audiences. The highest-profile example is Wabi, which raised $20 million last year to be the “YouTube of apps,” though it has since pivoted to be more of an app-powered personal AI agent (while raising another $55 million). The App Store is also awash in apps like Vibecode, Vibecoder, and VibeStudio, which look to varying degrees like they were made with AI themselves.

Harrington and Massena, who worked together on Microsoft Bob and later sold their photo editor startup Picnik to Google, are betting that a combination of social sharing features and their own expertise in software development will help Playful break through. Harrington also cofounded Valve Software, where he worked on the hit PC game Half-Life. The duo launched their startup in 2023 under the name Hatch, intending to offer a no-code platform for web apps, and pivoted to artificial intelligence after realizing how it would make app creation much more accessible.

“We’ve always gone after things that are consumer-oriented, and fun, and to a certain kind of audience,” Harrington says. “Picnik . . . grew from just a little photo editor to where we had 60 million monthly uniques, and about 85% of them were women. It’s just a market that people didn’t go after, and I think there’s a similar thing in apps.”

How Playful works

Creating an app in Playful starts with a simple question: “What kind of app do you want to make, and who’s it for?”

What happens next is where Playful distinguishes itself from a typical chatbot. Based on your original prompt, it will ask follow-up questions on things like the features you most care about and how you’ll use the app.

For instance, I asked Playful to build an audio transcription app that cleans up the text, identifies speakers, creates topic shortcuts to skip to, and lets you tap on the text to hear the corresponding audio. Playful in turn asked about recording scenarios—interviews, lectures, or personal voice notes—and whether I’d want to do things like access old interviews or export full transcripts.

“It helps you with the process because it understands a lot of things about apps, making apps, what might make sense, what’s popular in apps,” Massena says.

After a few minutes, Playful presents a smartphone-sized app that you can run through Playful’s own app or turn into a standalone icon on your home screen. The apps are web-based, so they work on any device, without distribution through any app store.

Behind the scenes, Harrington and Massena say that Playful uses a variety of large language models to fulfill users’ requests. Compared with using a more general-purpose AI tool, Harrington says Playful has more specific training on the process of creating apps and how to distill users’ requests. It also has built-in tools for things like data storage, and it can offer AI capabilities like summarization within the apps themselves. The ability to connect external data sources such as email and calendars is on the way.

“No one has to worry about ‘Where’s my stuff stored, what kind of database is needed for this?'” Massena says. “If you look at a lot of the other products out there . . . there’s still a lot of technical problems that you have to get comfortable with.”

That’s not to say a single prompt is always enough. With my attempt at a transcription tool, for instance, Playful’s app initially crashed out to a blank screen, and then tried to impose a 20-minute recording limit. After some working with Playful’s chatbot to solve those problems, it took some extra back-and-forth to get proper transcript formatting, and I gave up on trying to label speakers as it just never worked well.

Even so, the resulting app was helpful in reviewing my recorded interview for this story, and Harrington and Massena say they’ve been impressed with what early testers have come up with. One user, for instance, built an entire Excel-style spreadsheet editor for personal finance, while another built their own take on Capcut for AI video editing and captioning.

“It’s amazing what people have built out,” Massena says.

A new kind of app store

Playful’s apps aren’t just for individual use. Users can share their apps with others via a link or email invite, and they’ll automatically get updates when the creator pushes out new versions. Playful also supports sharing a “Copy” of the app—with separate data for each user—and “Remixing” so that others can modify the app as they wish.

Massena says the long-term vision is for those shared, editable apps to be the “new normal” for app distribution, versus the “take it or leave it” approach of conventional app stores.

“Why wouldn’t you go to a place where you could pull an app off the shelf, it was incredibly high-quality, full-featured, but that you could change any way you want to meet your needs?” he says. “That’s going to become the new normal for apps.”

The only point of friction in this argument is Playful’s business model, which strictly limits what users can do without a $10 per month subscription. After 30 days, Playful puts free users’ apps to sleep, and it bars them from creating more than two apps total.

Massena says Playful initially experimented with a different approach, in which users received a certain number of “credits” to use as they wished. But that just led to anxiety from testers around how many credits they were using. Even without a subscription, Playful does want to allow users to try other users’ apps, at least to some extent.

“Maybe you have a new inspiration, something there you want to try out, we’ll make sure that that’s always possible for people,” Massena says.

Whether or not Playful succeeds, it illustrates the uncharted territory where we’re heading with software. The iOS App Store is already seeing a boom in submissions, and Microsoft’s GitHub has been drastically increasing capacity due to a sixfold increase in code commits. Last month, the developer Brandon Thomas declared that “software is over” after using AI to spit out a series of lookalikes for popular apps like Adobe Photoshop and Microsoft Word.

What does the future of software look like when anyone can build a free version of an app they like that also better suits their needs? It’s unclear, but Massena and Harrington hope to be at the forefront of the answer.

“Software companies are going to have to be more responsive to people, or it’ll be much easier to find alternatives,” Massena says. “We’re building a platform for that new future.”

#10249. How Norway flipped Trump’s name-calling into destination marketing

After President Donald Trump called Norway a “shithouse country,” its tourism agency turned the insult into a marketing opportunity to promote its designer bathrooms.

Trump criticized Norway at a rally in Michigan on October 25 because he didn’t receive the Nobel Peace Prize, which is awarded by the Norwegian Nobel Committee. Disparaging the Nordic nation with a term he’s previously used for Haiti, ​Libya, Somalia, and Yemen, Trump said he didn’t want immigrants from Norway. Now its tourism agency has turned the attack into a badge of honor with a website for the world’s best toilets that’s drawing eyes from across the globe.

While Visit Norway has had a web page about its public toilets for several years owing to their dramatic views and better than average design, the group changed the headline of the page to reference Trump’s comments and reshared it last week. It’s currently Visit Norway’s most popular page in most countries and has had 200,000 page views since Monday, while related social media posts have generated 5 million organic views so far, Visit Norway tells Fast Company.

The updated web page says “Norway makes shithouses great again!” and shows off some of the country’s most scene-stealing public accommodations across Norwegian Scenic Routes, a collection of some of the 18 prettiest drives in the country.

Among them are the Stegastein Lookout restroom, which looks out over a fjord, was designed by the architects Todd Saunders and Tommie Wilhelmsen, and won a Norwegian National Construction Prize. The restroom at Ureddplassen, a seaside memorial designed by Haugen/Zohar Architects that honors those killed on a Norwegian submarine by a German mine during World War II, is housed inside a wave-shaped building made from poured concrete with frosted glass windows, and it’s been called “the world’s most beautiful public loo.”

“Along the Norwegian Scenic Routes, architecture and design are used deliberately to enhance the experience of traveling through some of Norway’s most dramatic landscapes,” says Visit Norway’s head of consumer marketing, Anne-Signe Fagereng. “Leading architects have designed rest stops, viewpoints, and public toilets that fit into the landscape. Many have won international architecture awards, and several have become attractions in their own right. Travelers come to see them, photograph them and, yes, use them.”

A well-designed stop takes pressure off nature, makes remote areas accessible to everyone, and turns a necessary break into part of the experience, she says.

What Visit Norway’s selected restrooms have in common is thoughtful architecture and prime locations, like the rest area at Flesefossen waterfall or the restrooms at Skjervsfossen, which has glass floors and windows that look out over a river and was designed by the architectural firm Fortunen. The Oslo-based firm Snøhetta designed its service building at a hill called Kvalhausen as if it’s coming out of the hill.

Americans marvel at the cleanliness of bathrooms at truck stops like Buc-ee’s or Maverick, but in Norway, the best public restrooms show what’s possible when a government really invests in their services. Norwegian Scenic Routes is run by the Norwegian Public Roads Administration, or Statens Vegvesen.

Visit Norway says the updated site isn’t a political statement or broader criticism of anyone specifically—it’s just destination marketing. And it seems to be working. The tourism agency says it’s received many positive messages from Americans who say they want to visit. Now thanks to Trump’s comments, rest stops are on their to-do list.

The company has been getting away with it for years, too.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Google just shut down a massive botnet operation involving an OEM and ODM manufacturer. According to the company blog, Videostrong Technology Co., which was a certified Android TV partner, purposefully installed a backdoor into 1.3 million set-top boxes and then sold access to criminal affiliates. This allowed for the installation of hidden software that the bad actors could use to conduct ad fraud, build residential proxy networks, and even remotely install malware on the device itself to target the end-user.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the company said in the Google Cloud blog post. It also added, “We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates. We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight. As a result, Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned them from making devices with preloaded Google apps.”

While Google did not mention when Videostrong started loading malware into its products, the company said that the pre-installed malware evolved into a complex, three-stage design in 2024. This meant that the manufacturer has been exploiting millions of devices for years now, with the latest developments designed to make the malware more resilient and allow for multiple bad actors to take advantage of the system. Even though the company has already terminated its business relationship with Videostrong, the open-source nature of Android means that it could continue using the operating system on its products.

There have been supply chain attacks in the past, wherein a third-party compromises a trusted product to steal data, like some Ledger hardware wallets that have been sold by a reseller in Southeast Asia and Europe. Although Google did not characterize this as a supply chain attack, as it was perpetrated by the manufacturer itself and not a third-party operator, it still compromised a supposedly trusted operating system, leading to millions of victims. This incident also shows how even the simplest of devices can be used to execute complicated attacks, like how a Chinese couple hid a PC behind a fridge in a Japanese hotel and targeted 2.4 million victims.

#10245. Bluesky was right all along and will accept your apology any time

Bluesky is a niche Twitter-clone frequently accused of being an echo chamber for progressives. After the blue tsunami of this week’s midterms, however, its inhabitants don’t seem to be echoing themselves so much as the vast majority of American voters.

The sheer scale of Democrats’ victory is staggering. They won control of both chambers of the U.S. Congress, flipping Senate seats in seven states Trump carried in 2024—including Republican stronghold Texas, which now also has a Democratic governor and attorney general. All in all, this year’s midterms represent the biggest electoral shift in state-level politics to hit the U.S. in generations. They also represent a Texas-sized validation of the worldview Bluesky has become notorious for over the past two years.

Although it officially launched in the spring of 2023, Bluesky might as well have been born on election eve in 2024. That was the moment millions of disillusioned Twitter users decamped from a website owned by the largest single contributor to Trump’s reelection. Bluesky quickly became a haven for Twitter expats and grew at a frenetic pace. It went from 9 million users in September 2024 to 15 million by mid-November, eventually reaching its current 47 million.

Because many of Bluesky’s users arrived out of principled opposition to X, formerly Twitter, the two sites have arguably existed in opposition to each other. Both portray their counterpart as out of touch, with Bluesky alleging Elon Musk’s algorithm tweaks have skewed X’s political vortex too far to the right, and X suggesting Bluesky is a bubble of liberals who can tolerate anything except a difference in opinion.

The latter idea seemed to largely prevail. 

In 2025, Washington Post columnists, tech world figures like Mark Cuban, and myriad other pundits dismissed Bluesky as smug, self-righteous, and irrelevant. It was the fantasy sandbox where progressives went to play among themselves, protecting reality dwellers from having to hear their drivel. (“Like a containment dome over a nuclear reactor,” as the writer Josh Barro put it.)

So, how well did Bluesky’s users stay in touch with reality between elections, compared with X’s exponentially larger population? Consider the post-midterms perspective.

Rather than accept the narrative that 2024 represented a rejection of “wokeness” and a political realignment toward Trump, the manifestly trans-friendly Bluesky suggested the election was more a referendum on postpandemic inflation and global anti-incumbent bias. As an emboldened Trump then proceeded to antagonize U.S. citizens and the rest of the world, while making billions for himself in crypto, Bluesky meticulously chronicled the state of play. It became the premier destination for seeing radicalized older white ladies, abysmally attended pro-ICE rallies, and complaints about the lack of mainstream news coverage around massive No Kings protests. Any random day would find endless posts with evidence that, per the motto of the political philosopher and Bluesky power user Olúfẹ́mi O. Táíwò, “We are going to win.” 

Above all, Bluesky proved to be less a bubble than an expression of the multitude of ideological factions that had united under the umbrella of non-MAGAness . . . to argue with one another.

Meanwhile, X’s millions of liberal and progressive folks were often drowned out by an algorithm that seemed to favor right-wing voices and their preferred narratives. A bubble chart from Nate Silver, the political analyst, visually depicted the accounts with highest engagement rates back in April. Its many MAGA-red circles made it look like the blood-filled elevator from The Shining. As a May 2026 study from Northwestern University suggests, X’s algorithm rewards posts that provoke strong reactions, so the loudest and most emotionally satisfying political claims become disproportionately visible. That’s how we got viral fever dreams about James Talarico, the then-senatorial candidate, checking into a mental hospital, something that never in fact happened.

It should come as little surprise that many high-profile MAGA voices on X spent the days leading up to the election incorrectly predicting how it would turn out.

Who looks out of touch and stuck in an echo chamber now?

While X may have been more plugged into the political discourse online for the past two years, Bluesky now appears better attuned to what’s been happening on the ground. Its users were right about pretty much everything. 

They were right that anti-trans ads would have little or no impact on the 2026 election, and that their impact on the previous election had been vastly overstated.

They were right that Graham Platner wasn’t the only Democrat who could beat Susan Collins in Maine, and that Abdul El-Sayed’s association with a controversial Twitch streamer relatively few voters had even heard of was not as big a deal as X users seemed to think. 

And they were right that fleeing X’s algorithm helped them view the world with clear eyes.

If Bluesky is a bubble, then it is currently a champagne bubble awash in celebration.

The festivities will likely last only a matter of hours, though, until infighting explodes around just how the Democrats should spend their newfound political capital.
