#10203. All the news about The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake

Ahead of the release of Rockstar Games’ Grand Theft Auto VI, Nintendo is launching its own fall juggernaut: a Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

The remake, which is releasing 28 years after the launch of the original version on Nintendo 64, has a much more realistic visual style and some modern improvements like a jump button, a way to sprint, full voice acting, and a “Threads of Time” feature that helps you keep track of your progress. But while the game has a new coat of paint, it appears many elements will still remain faithful to the classic N64 release. Nintendo has also launched a special version of the Switch 2 and Switch 2 Pro Controller with Triforce imagery to celebrate the game.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is scheduled to release on November 5th. You can follow along with all of our coverage of the game right here.

The Ocarina of Time remake on the Switch 2 smashes together the past and present. The game retains much of the original N64 experience while updating it with modern graphics and gameplay that make it feel contemporary. But the mingling of time periods also extends to the development team. While Ocarina’s remake was led by producers Eiji Aonuma (a director on the original game who is now the franchise’s steward at Nintendo) and Hidemaro Fujibayashi (best known for directing Breath of the Wild and its sequel), the team also featured a number of younger developers, including some who had never played the original. According to Fujibayashi, those new voices provided some much-needed perspective that shaped the remake.

“What really impressed me was the fact that they really embraced the theme of what not to change from the original,” Fujibayashi tells me ahead of Ocarina of Time’s launch when explaining the influence of the younger team members, who approached the project “very carefully.” He adds that “I feel confident that they weren’t necessarily pursuing something new for the sake of novelty when it might be unneeded and clutter the experience. They’re looking for elegance. Only what is needed, only what was important in the original, and how to carry that forward as their focus. And I think that’s a perspective they’ll be able to bring to future projects as well.”

Nintendo revealed yesterday that it held blind voice auditions for the Ocarina of Time remake and ended up casting an actor for the same role they had in the original. That actor was apparently Kaori Mizuhashi, who played Navi in the original and is listed as Navi’s Japanese voice in a leaked credits sequence for the remake, Eurogamer reports.

Breath of the Wild changed everything. Two decades after The Legend of Zelda made the transformational shift to 3D, Breath of the Wild reinvigorated the franchise with an open-ended adventure that was built around player freedom and expression. Instead of following a set path, players could go wherever they wanted and tackle challenges in a variety of ways. That philosophy filtered down to subsequent games, letting players author their own creative solutions to puzzles in titles like Tears of the Kingdom and Echoes of Wisdom. As a result, Zelda has never been bigger, and the traditional, more linear Zelda games had become a thing of the past. Or so it seemed.

For one of the biggest Switch 2 exclusives so far, Nintendo has gone back to Ocarina of Time, which originally launched on the N64 in 1998. It’s one of the most influential and revered games in the long-running franchise, a game that showed that the classic Zelda formula — one that used a large world to connect a handful of intricate, puzzle-filled dungeons, creating a grand adventure — could work in three dimensions. Now Ocarina has been remade for the Switch 2 in a way that accomplishes exactly what a good remake is designed to do: preserve the core of the original experience while making it more accessible for modern audiences. And it shows there’s still some life left in the traditional Zelda formula.

For the Ocarina of Time remake, Nintendo developers said in a new interview that they wanted to “preserve the experience of spamming the Roll Attack to forward roll your way across Hyrule Field.” I have very fond memories of rolling around the world in the original.

In the remake, you can still spam Roll Attack, but you can also dash.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time launches later this week, and in the lead-up Nintendo has put out the first half of a lengthy developer Q&A, covering everything from what changed gameplay-wise, to the new visual style, which was inspired by puppet shows. As art director Aya Shida explains:

Neither puppet shows nor practical effects films reproduce reality exactly as it is. Even so, both create a convincing sense that the characters truly exist within their respective fantasy worlds. We also felt that there was some overlap between these forms of expression and the distinctive nostalgia evoked by the original game.

The two biggest games of 2026 are set to launch just a few weeks apart in November.

The long-awaited remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Nintendo Switch 2 launches next Thursday, November 5th. In other words, you have a week remaining to secure your physical edition with a $10 discount at Amazon and Walmart. Once the game launches, the physical version will almost certainly go from $59.99 to $69.99 while the digital version will stay at $59.99.

Nintendo had the unenviable task of reimagining its Nintendo 64-era masterpiece for the Switch 2, and based on our hands-on time with some sections of the game, it’s a lot of fun to play. The graphics and art style are fantastic, and the controls have been modernized to be simpler to pick up for those who are already experienced with third-person action games, including other modern Zelda titles.

I’ve really warmed up to the game’s art style, especially in this new trailer. And after reading my colleague Cameron Faulkner’s hands-on preview, I’m looking forward to returning to Hyrule even more. The game launches on Switch 2 on November 5th.

With its upcoming remake for the Switch 2, Nintendo might have nailed the best thing about The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time: its timelessness. The 1998 3D action adventure game for the Nintendo 64 that pioneered so much — 3D graphics, movement, exploration, openness — has been reengineered with changes that make it feel more modern, and surprisingly terrifying at times. Based on my early hands-on time with the game, it’s shaping up to be the best-looking, best-playing version of the game that addresses the most frustrating aspects of playing the original.

More than just sanding off its roughest edges, Nintendo also fitted Ocarina of Time with modern trappings to make it more welcoming to those who were introduced to Zelda through more modern releases, like Breath of the Wild. The remake has a new progression marker, called Threads of Time, that’s viewable when you pause. It also has Zelda Notes integration within the Nintendo Switch app to let you view game maps and other info on your phone. Oh, it also has a dedicated jump button.

It was briefly shown during Nintendo’s The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Direct today, but Hori’s website now has a listing for its $49.99 electronic ocarina. You can play your own songs by pushing buttons, play one of 12 pre-programmed songs from the games, use it with the Ocarina of Time remake’s sound recognition feature, or connect headphones for a private jam session.

Link’s next adventure now has a release date. During a Legend of Zelda stream for the franchise’s 40th anniversary, Nintendo announced that the upcoming Ocarina of Time remake for the Switch 2 is launching on November 5th. The release date makes Ocarina of Time one of just a few big-budget titles launching in the same month as Grand Theft Auto VI.

Nintendo first teased the remake in June, though it didn’t reveal much aside from a brief trailer. Today’s event provided a clearer glimpse at how the company is approaching remaking one of its most influential games and the first 3D Zelda adventure. The updated version of Ocarina of Time will be the first Zelda release that’s exclusive to the Switch 2, and longtime Zelda producer Eiji Aonuma described the remake as “a faithful interpretation using modern technologies.”

Tuesday’s Nintendo Direct showcase felt like an important moment for the company. With the Switch 2 heading into its second holiday season, one in which the hardware will be even more expensive thanks to a price hike, it was a chance for Nintendo to really sell new audiences on its latest console — but that’s not exactly what happened. While there were some impressive-looking titles, there wasn’t much that felt truly new. Instead, the two major Switch 2 exclusives that will round out the 2026 calendar are both remakes from the Nintendo 64 era.

If you missed it, the final reveal of the Direct was a remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Switch 2. We don’t know when, exactly, it’s launching, but Nintendo says it’ll be out this year. The brief teaser didn’t reveal much of what the game will look like, nor how it might differ from the N64 original, so chances are you can expect an Ocarina-focused Direct in the coming months that will detail more. Whenever it comes out, the Ocarina remake will follow the Star Fox remake, which is launching later this month in an attempt to revitalize Nintendo’s long-dormant sci-fi series for modern audiences.

Nintendo announced a remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time during its Nintendo Direct presentation on Tuesday. It will launch sometime in 2026 on Nintendo Switch 2. More details will be announced “in the future.”

This new title is the first major release in the franchise since 2024’s Echoes of Wisdom, which starred Princess Zelda herself. Echoes followed 2023’s Tears of the Kingdom, a direct sequel to Breath of the Wild — both of which got upgraded Switch 2 versions alongside the launch of the new console last year. In November, Nintendo also launched the hack-and-slash title Hyrule Warriors: Age of Imprisonment.

#10202. Holotron-12B - High Throughput Computer Use Agent

We're thrilled to release Holotron-12B, a multimodal computer-use model from H Company. Post-trained from the open NVIDIA Nemotron-Nano-2 VL model on H Company’s proprietary data mixture, Holotron-12B is the result of a close collaboration between our research labs to engineer a new type of model optimized primarily for scale and performance in production.

H Company is part of the NVIDIA Inception Program.

The model is now available on Hugging Face.

Most multimodal models today optimize primarily for static vision or following instructions. Holotron-12B, just like our Holo2 model, however, has a different goal: serving as a policy model for computer-use agents that must perceive, decide, and act efficiently in interactive environments.

With Holotron-12B, we wanted to create a model that could efficiently and effectively scale in production while handling long contexts with multiple images, and still perform well on agent benchmarks. The NVIDIA Nemotron model offered a strong foundation on the inference side, and by developing Holotron-12B we've demonstrated how much more the model can accomplish with further training.

Holotron-12B's significant leap in inference efficiency is made possible by its foundational Nemotron architecture, which utilizes a hybrid State-Space Model (SSM) and attention mechanism. Unlike purely transformer-based models, this design is optimized for high-throughput serving. State-space models offer superior scalability for long-context inference by avoiding the quadratic computation cost associated with the full attention mechanism, particularly benefiting agentic workloads involving multiple images and lengthy interaction histories. In terms of inference, the main contribution of an SSM is its dramatically reduced memory-footprint: while vanilla attention stores K and V activations per token and layer (the notorious KV Cache), SSMs are a linear recurrent model, storing only a constant state per layer per generated sequence, independent of the length of the sequence.

When evaluated on the WebVoyager Benchmark, the model excels using a real-world multimodal agentic workload featuring long context, multiple high-resolution images, and a high request concurrency of 100 benchmark workers. Running on a single H100 GPU and using vLLM with the latest SSM optimizations (v0.14.1), Holotron-12B achieved an over 2x higher throughput compared to Holo2-8B. This makes Holotron-12B an attractive choice for throughput-bound workloads, such as data generation, annotation, and online reinforcement learning.

In a controlled experiment setup (see figure 2), Holotron-12B continues to scale efficiently as concurrency increases, with total token throughput rising steadily to 8.9k tokens/s at a max concurrency of 100. In contrast, the total token throughput of Holo2-8B plateaus much more quickly at 5.1k tokens/s. This behaviour highlights a key strength of the Nemotron architecture, namely more effective and efficient VRAM utilization, and smaller overall memory footprint, which allows much larger effective batch sizes on the same hardware. Even at large batch sizes, Holotron-12B maintains strong throughput.

Holotron-12B was trained in two stages. We started from Nemotron-Nano-12B-v2-VL-BF16, a multimodal base model published by NVIDIA. We then performed supervised fine-tuning on H Company’s proprietary localization and navigation data mixture, focusing on screen understanding, grounding, and UI-level interactions.

The final checkpoint was trained on approximately 14 billion tokens.

On computer-use and navigation benchmarks, Holotron-12B shows strong improvements over the Nemotron base model and strong performance with established agent models. Its WebVoyager performance increased from 35.1% to 80.5%, exceeding Holo2-8B’s performance on the benchmark and illustrating the model’s ability to perform effectively in an agentic setting.

Holotron-12B also improves substantially over the base Nemotron model on localization and grounding benchmarks such as OS-World-G, GroundUI, and WebClick.

Holotron-12B demonstrates that the NVIDIA Nemotron VL model provides a strong foundation for real-world multimodal agents when paired with the right training setup and infrastructure work.

The model offers strong agent performance, significantly improved inference throughput, and a clear path for future improvements, particularly around higher-resolution vision training.

We look forward to seeing what others build with Holotron-12B. The model and checkpoints are available now on Hugging Face under an NVIDIA Open Model License.

NVIDIA announced today the release of Nemotron 3 Omni. Building on the success of Holotron-12B, we are preparing to post-train this next generation of multimodal models. By leveraging the enhanced hybrid SSM-Attention and MoE architectural foundations of the Nemotron 3 family, we aim to deliver even greater leaps in reasoning capabilities and multimodal precision with the newly announced Nemotron 3 Omni. As this evolution pushes Holotron beyond research and into a commercial application, it will provide enterprises with the high-throughput, low-latency performance required for massive-scale autonomous "computer use" deployments.

North Korean hackers targeted two Binance employees on the way to a $6.3 billion heist

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Binance has revealed how North Korean hackers spent months preparing to steal approximately $6.34 billion in cryptocurrency last week. According to a November 3 security report by the exchange, the attackers used a malicious Homebrew installation to compromise one engineer and a fake recruitment process to trick another into installing malware disguised as a coding assistant. "Our current investigation indicates that this was a sophisticated, multi-stage campaign. It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident," the exchange said.

Binance says the first known compromise occurred in June, when an engineer in Binance’s Wallet DevOps team searched online for a popular AI coding tool and downloaded an adulterated Homebrew installation. Homebrew is a package manager, used by developers to install and manage various software tools on macOS.

Binance says it detected the unusual activity, replaced the engineer’s device, and rotated their associated credentials. However, those moves proved to be too little, too late, as the attackers had already learned about the employee’s role and identified colleagues working on the exchange's wallet infrastructure

The incident follows the compromise of another Binance software engineer who was contacted in September through a legitimate job hunting platform by a malicious actor posing as a project director. The fake recruiter arranged two interviews. One involved a purported HR representative who conducted a live video call and shared a social media account containing personal photos and videos to establish credibility, while the second involved someone posing as a CEO of a fictitious company.

Near the end of the interview, the engineer was asked to download a coding assignment containing a malicious software repository onto his work computer—a popular social engineering scheme. That malicious code executed during the setup process. At the time, Binance said the malware replaced a legitimate component of the Python version-management tool "pvenv" with a malicious version capable of executing commands and communicating with an attacker-controlled server. The exchange's endpoint security tools did not detect the malware at the time.

Those compromises began bearing fruit on October 20, as the attackers used the compromised computers associated with the fake interview and an internal AI tool to gain control over two wallet engineers' devices. They also discovered a container deployment permission token stored on the computer of the engineer initially targeted in June.

Later, on October 29, the attackers used stolen credentials to access another engineer's computer, deploy a container, and execute a malicious script. This gave them access to Binance's internal wallet signing service, allowing transactions from five hot wallets outside the exchange's normal withdrawal process.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The U.S. FBI directly attributed the theft to North Korea on November 1. ”The FBI is releasing information advising the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange, Binance, on or about October 29, 2026. The FBI refers to this specific North Korean malicious cyber activity as "TraderTraitor," the agency tweeted. Pyongyang has distanced itself from the hack, describing the U.S. claims as "preposterous nonsense.”

Binance said it had since frozen or intercepted approximately $2.85 billion in compromised assets, while 98% of the affected funds have been replenished.

The tactics resemble previous North Korean-linked campaigns. WaterPlum attackers previously used fake job postings and coding tests to infect more than 30,000 devices across 100 countries, compromising over 7,000 crypto wallets in September. A 2024 campaign that targeted Python developers with fake job offers and malware hidden in code was attributed to the Lazarus group, which was also linked to the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in 2025. Attackers posed as potential employers and sent coding tests containing Base64 obfuscated malware. Running the tests could infect developers' computers, giving attackers remote access.

#10199. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time never gets old

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The franchise has evolved since 1998, but the first 3D Zelda stands up incredibly well in its Switch 2 remake.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Breath of the Wild changed everything. Two decades after The Legend of Zelda made the transformational shift to 3D, Breath of the Wild reinvigorated the franchise with an open-ended adventure that was built around player freedom and expression. Instead of following a set path, players could go wherever they wanted and tackle challenges in a variety of ways. That philosophy filtered down to subsequent games, letting players author their own creative solutions to puzzles in titles like Tears of the Kingdom and Echoes of Wisdom. As a result, Zelda has never been bigger, and the traditional, more linear Zelda games had become a thing of the past. Or so it seemed.

For one of the biggest Switch 2 exclusives so far, Nintendo has gone back to Ocarina of Time, which originally launched on the N64 in 1998. It’s one of the most influential and revered games in the long-running franchise, a game that showed that the classic Zelda formula — one that used a large world to connect a handful of intricate, puzzle-filled dungeons, creating a grand adventure — could work in three dimensions. Now Ocarina has been remade for the Switch 2 in a way that accomplishes exactly what a good remake is designed to do: preserve the core of the original experience while making it more accessible for modern audiences. And it shows there’s still some life left in the traditional Zelda formula.

The story remains unchanged from the original. It’s a third-person action-adventure game where you play as a little forest dweller named Link who gets pulled into an adventure to save the fantasy realm of Hyrule from a villain named Ganondorf. That’s true of basically every Zelda title, and here the twist comes from a musical instrument (the titular flute-like ocarina) imbued with magical powers. Over the course of the game you learn songs that can change the weather, warp you across the landscape, mess with the flow of time, and more.

The original Ocarina was renowned both for its large 3D world and for the intricacy of its dungeons, which required using the ocarina, along with various other items, to solve puzzles in clever ways. At a certain point you’re even jumping back and forth in time, navigating spaces as both tiny Link and his adult version. The challenge steadily grows in complexity right up until you face Ganondorf in his castle, forcing you to use a huge range of items at your disposal.

The most notable difference in the remake is how it looks. Gone are the blocky, fuzzy N64-era graphics, which have been replaced with something that blurs the line between fantasy art and realism. While it’s not a fully open world like Breath of the Wild, this version of Hyrule, which has a large open field that connects a series of dungeons and villages, is still incredibly lifelike; everything from rushing water in a lake to the swaying grass outside of a ranch looks and moves in realistic ways. The flip side is that, while the characters are more detailed than before, they’ve been rendered with a style inspired by puppets and stage shows. It’s a tricky balancing act that the game mostly nails. The characters look like exaggerated caricatures, but at the same time they’re imbued with such a level of detail that they don’t feel out of place against the more realistic backdrops. Link is the best example; while his face almost looks like a porcelain figure, his outfit is like something a real adventurer would wear, made by weaving together grasses found in Kokiri Forest, where he lives.

It looks great in practice — although Ocarina does suffer from some frustratingly dark areas, like in most modern games — and it also sets the remake apart from the rest of modern Zelda adventures. The Breath of the Wild line has a fantastical, Studio Ghibli-inspired look, while the top-down spinoffs have cutesy, toylike graphics. Ocarina splits the difference and comes out looking like something distinct, yet unmistakably Zelda. The Switch 2 graphics also do a great job of heightening the emotion. There’s an incredible sense of grandeur when you first walk into the stark Temple of Time, with a single ray of light illuminating the dark interior. Iconic moments like wandering blindly through the desert take on a new sense of tension and terror because of how the game looks as sand whips around you, obscuring your view of the harsh landscape. Fighting Dark Link on a foggy, desolate beach was enough to get my heart racing.

Perhaps more important than the visual update is a number of smart gameplay changes. Early 3D games can be awkward to play now because designers were still working out how best to navigate 3D spaces. The Ocarina remake fixes this in a few ways. For one thing, you now have free camera control, making it possible to look anywhere by moving the right stick, just like in any modern game. This makes it easier to keep your eye on enemies around you or spot important details for solving a puzzle. The game now also lets you jump whenever you want — in the original Link could only jump at designated points — which makes moving around in spaces feel less restrictive. Other modern touches include being able to equip items quickly with the D-pad instead of having to go to the pause menu, and the “threads of time,” which is a fancy name for a tool that tracks your quests so you can more easily figure out what to do next.

As an example of how much these tweaks can impact the experience, let’s revisit the infamous Water Temple. Over the years since Ocarina of Time first launched, this dungeon has become known primarily for being extremely difficult. It involves constantly playing a song to make the water rise and fall so you can access different levels, while also frequently equipping iron boots that cause Link to sink to the bottom when necessary. With the original controls this was tedious and frustrating. But I didn’t find it difficult at all in the remake; I could quickly equip the boots whenever I needed to, and the camera allowed me to clearly see what I needed to do. The Water Temple was always a well-designed dungeon hindered by the technology of the time. In the remake, I could fully appreciate what the developers were going for.

There are a handful of other changes — expanded dialogue, the ability to hum songs into the Switch 2’s microphone, the fairy Navi thankfully toning down her annoying hints — and they all build toward the same goal: enhancing the original without changing its essence. Unlike a lot of classic games, the original Ocarina of Time is still relatively easy to play; it’s available through a Switch Online subscription, and the 3DS version from 2011 remains a great port. But the remake does enough to make it the ideal way to play, particularly for that big new audience of Zelda fans that started with Breath of the Wild. More importantly, it’s proof that Zelda can be many things simultaneously. And that’s an exciting prospect for Hyrule’s future.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time launches on the Switch 2 on November 5th.

#10198. How Product Teams Can Use AI User Research to Test Assumptions Before Sprint Planning

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sprint planning is on Thursday, and the top of the backlog rests on three things nobody has checked. Users want the feature, they will find it, and they will understand what it does when they do. Each belief is plausible, and each has already been written into a ticket.

AI user research uses language models to simulate or analyze user conversations, so a team can put a question to a modeled audience in minutes instead of recruiting people for weeks. Used well, it gives a product team a cheap first check on backlog assumptions. Used badly, it produces confident-sounding agreement. This guide covers a two-day routine that gets the benefit and avoids the trap.

An assumption is worth testing when the plan depends on it and a wrong answer would change the ticket. "Users like clean interfaces" fails that test. "Analysts re-apply the same filters every session" passes, because if it is false the saved-filters feature shrinks or disappears.

The timing matters because planning leaves little room for research. The Scrum Guide says Sprint Planning is timeboxed to a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint, and the first question the team answers is why the Sprint is valuable. Checks run before that meeting inform the answer. Checks run during it eat the time meant for deciding.

Write each risky item as a short card that names the belief, the consequence of being wrong, and the decision it feeds. A card forces the team to say what would change its mind, which most tickets never do. Here is an example:

Aim for three to five cards. A team that tries to test the whole backlog will test none of it, and the cards on the riskiest items give the best return.

AI user research comes in two forms. The first analyzes data you already hold: clustering support tickets and summarizing interview transcripts. It works on real evidence, so its main risk is a sloppy summary.

The second form interviews simulated people. AI user research of this kind builds a panel of modeled personas matched to your target profile, asks them your questions, and reports the themes. It needs no recruiting and returns results quickly, which fits a two-day window. Its output comes from a model of users and not from users, and that distinction should appear in every planning document that cites it.

A simulated audience helps most when you want to sharpen a question, and least when you need proof. Nielsen Norman Group's 2024 review of synthetic users found them useful for generating hypotheses and preparing interview guides. It warned against using them for final decisions or concept validation, and for niche populations, because AI tends to please and "every idea is often seen as a good one."

Spend Tuesday collecting answers and Wednesday reading them skeptically. On Tuesday, put each card's question to the modeled audience in neutral wording, and ask what would make them not use the feature. A question phrased as "Would saved filters help you?" invites a yes, while "Walk me through setting up your weekly report" does not.

On Wednesday, compare the answers with what you already know from support tickets and analytics. Mark each assumption as supported, contradicted, or unclear. Treat a unanimous answer with suspicion, because real audiences rarely agree on anything. Also be wary of lists in which the modeled users "seem to care about everything," which is how Nielsen Norman Group describes their weak prioritization.

Whatever stays unclear or high risk goes to real people. Jakob Nielsen's classic analysis found that five users find about 85% of usability problems, assuming comparable users, and he recommended several small rounds over one large one. An AI check is a good way to decide what those five people should be asked.

Each mark maps to a different decision. A contradicted assumption means the ticket is cut or reduced to its smallest useful version. A supported assumption that rests only on simulated evidence is not yet safe, so schedule a real-user check as the first task in the sprint, ahead of the build work that depends on it. An unclear assumption should not receive full scope.

The cost of skipping this step is real. A 2019 analysis of 615 product subscriptions by a product analytics vendor found that about 12% of features generate 80% of daily usage volume, and 80% of features are rarely or never used. That is one vendor's customer base, and the figures cover features that customers chose to track, so treat them as a rough guide. They still suggest that most of a backlog is a bet.

AI user research cannot replace talking to real users. Nielsen Norman Group found that synthetic users gave overly optimistic accounts of their own behavior, such as claiming to finish every course in a study, and that they cannot supply real past experience. It also called presenting synthetic findings as real-user findings "an unethical way to share what you've learned."

Two habits keep a team honest. Label every piece of evidence in the planning document as modeled, observed, or reported, and require that any feature built on modeled evidence has a real-user check scheduled. The review also warned that teams starting with synthetic research may get comfortable and skip the real kind, so put the real check on the calendar before the first AI result arrives.

Can AI user research replace interviews with real users? No. It is a cheap first pass that helps you write better questions and spot weak assumptions. Anything that drives a significant build still needs real people.

How many assumptions should a team test before planning? Three to five. Pick the ones where a wrong answer would cut or reshape a ticket.

How do I stop simulated users from just agreeing with me? Use neutral, open questions, ask what would make them avoid the feature, and treat unanimous answers as a warning sign.

What should I do with results I cannot verify? Mark them as modeled, give them less weight than observed evidence, and schedule a real-user check before committing full scope.

Sources: Scrum Guide, Sprint Planning; Jakob Nielsen, "Why You Only Need to Test with 5 Users" (March 18, 2000); Nielsen Norman Group, "Synthetic Users: If, When, and How to Use AI-Generated 'Research'" (June 21, 2024); 2019 Feature Adoption Report (615 product subscriptions, vendor-reported).

#10196. State of Open Source on Hugging Face: Spring 2026

This post examines how the open source AI landscape has shifted across competition, geography, technical trends, and emerging communities over the past year. We primarily examine community activity on Hugging Face across many types of metrics to give a holistic view of the ecosystem.

This post builds on an earlier analysis conducted mid-2025, available here, which examined what the Hugging Face Community is building. We recommend reading additional perspectives on the open source ecosystem in and outside of Hugging Face from the Data Provenance Initiative, Interconnects, OpenRouter and a16z, and MIT and the Linux Foundation. As the Hugging Face ecosystem is distributed, analyses are a combination of Hugging Face and community members' work, each of which is appropriately credited.

Activity in the open source AI ecosystem has rapidly grown, with the number of users, model, and dataset repositories all close to doubling. In 2025, Hugging Face grew to 13 million users, more than 2 million public models, and over 500,000 public datasets. This growth signals more than increased interest in open source; it reflects a shift toward active participation, with users increasingly creating derivative artifacts such as fine-tuned models, adapters, benchmarks, and applications rather than only consuming pre-trained systems.

Data from Hugging Face | Hugging Face's two million models and counting: Graph and story by AI World

The ecosystem remains highly concentrated. Approximately half of the models on Hugging Face have less than 200 total downloads, and the top 200 most downloaded models, or 0.01% of models, comprise 49.6% of all downloads.

Specialized communities form around particular domains, languages, or problem areas, and often show sustained engagement and reuse even when their overall download counts are modest. Open source AI is best understood as a collection of overlapping sub-ecosystems rather than a single uniform market.

More companies, both large and small, are building on open source. Over 30% of the Fortune 500 now maintain verified accounts on Hugging Face. Startups frequently use open models as default components: Thinking Machines built its Tinker model options entirely on open weights, while popular IDEs such as VSCode and Cursor support both open and closed models. Established American companies such as Airbnb have increased their engagement with the open ecosystem, and Hugging Face has seen more legacy companies upgrading their organizational subscriptions over the course of 2025.

Big Tech companies are frequently creating new repositories on Hugging Face Hub; visualized side-by-side, the strong increase in repository growth shows investment over time. NVIDIA has emerged as the strongest contributor.

Data from Hugging Face | Big Tech Is All-In On Open-Source AI, Graph and story by AI World

Studies of open software more broadly suggest that the downstream value created by open artifacts far exceeds the cost of producing them. Similar dynamics are emerging in AI, where open models are reused, adapted, and specialized across thousands of downstream applications. Organizations that rely exclusively on closed systems often incur higher costs and face reduced flexibility in deployment and customization.

All-time downloads over the past four years show clear frontrunner regions in model popularity. The U.S. and China have historically been top contributors, with the UK, Germany, and France as secondary in popularity. Models developed by individual users or distributed organizations without a clear geographic base account for about half of all platform downloads.

Data from Hugging Face | Graph and Research from Longpre et al. “Economies of Open Intelligence: Tracing Power & Participation in the Model Ecosystem”

The geographic composition of the open source ecosystem has fundamentally changed. Hugging Face data shows China surpassing the U.S. in monthly downloads and overall downloads. In the past year, Chinese models quickly accounted for the plurality or 41% of downloads.

Industry's share of overall development fell from around 70% before 2022 to roughly 37% in 2025. Meanwhile, independent or unaffiliated developers rose from 17% to 39% of all downloads over the same period, at times accounting for more than half of total usage. Individuals and small collectives focused on quantizing, adapting, and redistributing base models. These intermediaries now steer a meaningful portion of what typical users can run and how innovations spread through the ecosystem.

Data from Hugging Face | Graph and Research from Longpre et al. “Economies of Open Intelligence: Tracing Power & Participation in the Model Ecosystem”

Different regions contribute in different ways. The United States and Western Europe have historically dominated through large industry labs (Google, Meta, OpenAI, Stability AI), while China has increasingly led on both releases and adoption. France, Germany, and the UK continue to contribute through research organizations, national AI initiatives, and specialized model families. Ecosystems supporting a variety of contributors and organizational forms tend to produce more widely adopted artifacts.

Popular models from startups were more widespread. Competitive countries were France and South Korea. Notably, the fourth most popular entity for developing new trending models were individual users, not organizations. Creating competitive models at a user level is more accessible than ever before.

Of the newly created models in 2025, the majority of trending models were either developed in China or derivative of a model developed in China. The most popular models were developed by large organizations, predominantly from the U.S. and China. For more on the Chinese AI ecosystem, read our three part series reflecting on the changes in one year since the "DeepSeek Moment", with one on strategic changes, two on architectural changes, and three on organizations and the future.

In 2025, China’s AI ecosystem steered heavily into open source, following the viral release of DeepSeek’s R1 model in January. The number of competitive Chinese organizations releasing models and the number of repositories on Hugging Face skyrocketed. Baidu went from zero releases on the Hub in 2024 to over 100 in 2025. ByteDance and Tencent each increased releases by eight to nine times. Organizations that had previously favored closed approaches, including Baidu and MiniMax, shifted decisively toward open releases.

A similar number of popular U.S. organizations have consistently contributed a higher volume of repositories over time. Meta and its former Facebook research organization account for a significant proportion of open releases, as does Google to a lesser extent.

Next to each other, the steep upward trajectory of repository growth among popular Chinese organizations emerges as a key strategic difference.

Open source AI is increasingly tied to questions of sovereignty. Open weight models allow governments and public institutions to fine-tune systems on local data under national legal frameworks. Models that can be deployed on domestic hardware reduce reliance on foreign-controlled cloud infrastructure. Transparency around model architecture, training processes, and evaluation supports regulatory review and public accountability. Read more about the open source approach to sovereignty here.

At the national level, governments are taking action. South Korea's National Sovereign AI Initiative launched mid-2025 named national champions LG AI Research, SK Telecom, Naver Cloud, NC AI, and Upstage to produce competitive domestic models. Three models from South Korea trended simultaneously on Hugging Face Hub in February 2026. In March 2026, In 2026, South Korea and U.S. startup Reflection AI announced a data center partnership, also bringing frontier open weight models to South Korea.

Switzerland's Swiss AI initiative and various EU-funded projects reflect similar priorities. The UK's principle of "public money, public code" has influenced several government-backed AI initiatives.

These investments in open-source and open weight AI are already paying dividends for countries with thriving AI training ecosystems of their own, as we see that models and datasets are typically most used in the regions where they're developed; with developers often turning to the models that best represent their languages and reflect similar technical and application requirements.

Most liked models on the Hub show community attention, in terms of ability to go back to or reference the model or general popularity. While this metric does not always reflect usage, the attention collected over time can show signals of interest. In one year, the most liked models went from predominantly U.S.-developed from Meta’s Llama family, to an international mix with China’s DeepSeek-R1 at the top.

While determining the value of scientific contributions can be determined by many metrics, our upvote feature on the Hub shows papers from large AI organizations be widely appreciated by community members. Notably, the most upvoted papers are from large organizations, mostly from the U.S. and China. The majority of the top organizations are Chinese Big Tech companies, with ByteDance sharing a high volume of high impact papers.

Space by Hugging Face | PaperVerse Explorer

Of Hugging Face's Daily Papers, a set of papers curated by Hugging Face's AK, papers that reference model and dataset creation, showing the most open source adoption, are generally diverse. Prominent takeaways show medical papers being influential, while Big Tech's influence is sparse.

Data from Hugging Face | Graphic and story by AI World

How our community members choose to build on models, whether via fine-tuning, merging, or other methods, reflects model popularity and usability. Alibaba as an organization has more derivative models than both Google and Meta combined, with the Qwen family constituting more than 113,000 derivative models. When including all models that tag Qwen, that number balloons to over 200,000 models.

Model development has increasingly emphasized accessibility alongside scale. Smaller models are downloaded and deployed at far higher rates than very large systems, reflecting practical constraints around cost, latency, and hardware availability.

This small-model dominance occurs in part because far more models are released at that size. But even when normalizing for this, the data from the ATOM Project's Relative Adoption Metric shows that the median top-10 models from 1-9B parameters are only downloaded about 4x more than models above 100B. Automated systems and CI pipelines further inflate small model download counts, but the trend toward smaller, deployable models is real.

Data from Hugging Face | Graph and Article by ATOM

Engagement with open models tends to peak almost immediately after release, then slow. Mean engagement duration is approximately 6 weeks. Continuous improvement and frequent updates have become critical for maintaining relevance. DeepSeek's successive releases (V3, R1, V3.2) kept it competitive even as challengers emerged. Organizations that stagnate in development tend to lose share quickly to those with frequent updates or domain-specific fine-tunes.

Data from Hugging Face | Graph and Research from Choksi et al. "The Brief and Wondrous Life of Open Models"

The mean size of downloaded open models rose from 827M parameters in 2023 to 20.8B in 2025, driven largely by quantization and mixture-of-experts architectures. The median, however, increased only marginally, from 326M to 406M parameters. This divergence indicates that high-end LLM users are pulling up the mean while underlying small-model usage remains stable.

Data from Hugging Face | Graph and Research from Longpre et al. "Economies of Open Intelligence: Tracing Power & Participation in the Model Ecosystem"

Performance differences between frontier models and smaller systems often narrow rapidly through fine-tuning and task-specific adaptation. On the Hub, models with hundreds of millions of parameters support search, tagging, and document processing workflows, while models in the single-digit billions are widely used for coding, reasoning, and multimodal tasks. As a result, most major model developers now release families of models spanning a range of sizes. The rise of capable small models shifts autonomy closer to the edge, reducing dependency on centralized cloud providers.

Open source AI development is closely linked to hardware trends. Most models are optimized for NVIDIA GPUs, but support for AMD hardware continues to expand. Stability AI model collections now optimize for both NVIDIA and AMD platforms. Libraries increasingly target both, and tooling has improved to make cross-hardware deployment more straightforward. In 2025 Hugging Face launched the Kernel Hub to load and run kernels optimized for NVIDIA and AMD GPUs.

In parallel, Chinese open models are being released with explicit support for domestically developed chips. Alibaba has invested in inference-focused chip architectures designed to fill Chinese data centers with hardware capable of running open source models locally.

While access to compute remains a core necessity across the board for development and deployment of AI models, open-source and open-weight models are helping break away from an ecosystem where it becomes the be-all and end-all, with increasingly more models at all levels of performance pushing efficiency from 10x to 1000x lower costs than flagship AI models the largest developers.

Still, the question of infrastructure investment for open source remains urgent. Public funding for data centers capable of training and serving open models has become a growing policy discussion, particularly in Europe and the UK. The gap between the compute resources available to large closed-model companies and those accessible to the open source community continues to shape what is feasible in open development.

Robotics has emerged as one of the fastest-growing sub-communities on Hugging Face. The numbers are striking: robotics datasets grew from 1,145 in 2024 to 26,991 in 2025, climbing from rank 44 to the single largest dataset category on the Hub in just three years. For comparison, text generation, the second-largest category, had only around 5,000 datasets in 2025.

Data from Hugging Face | Graph and Story by AI World

Community-contributed datasets span everything from household manipulation tasks to autonomous driving. The largest multimodal dataset for spatial intelligence, Learning to Drive (L2D), was released through a LeRobot collaboration with Yaak. Datasets like RoboMIND, with over 107,000 real-world trajectories across 479 distinct tasks and multiple robot embodiments, provide the kind of scale and diversity needed for training generalizable robotic policies.

Hugging Face's acquisition of Pollen Robotics opened open source robotic sales to both industry and academic labs, as well as everyday hobbyists. LeRobot, Hugging Face's open source robotics library that provides models, datasets, and tools for real-world robotics in PyTorch, covering imitation learning, reinforcement learning, and vision-language-action models, experienced rapid growth. Over the past year, its GitHub repository stars nearly tripled.

Data from GitHub | Graphic from star-history.com

Scientific research has become another particularly active area. Open models and datasets are increasingly used for protein folding, molecular dynamics, drug discovery, and scientific data analysis. All frontier AI companies now have dedicated science teams, though much current focus remains on literature discovery rather than direct experimentation.

Space by Hugging Face | Science Release Heatmap

Community-led projects have formed around shared research goals, often involving hundreds of contributors working across institutions and disciplines. These efforts highlight the role of open source as a mechanism for coordinating large-scale, interdisciplinary work that would be difficult to organize through traditional academic or corporate structures alone.

The open source AI ecosystem continues to evolve through a combination of global participation, technical specialization, and institutional adoption. Several trends are likely to define the next phase.

The geographic rebalancing of power is accelerating. Western organizations increasingly seek commercially deployable alternatives to Chinese models, creating urgency around efforts like OpenAI's GPT-OSS, AI2's OLMo, and Google's Gemma to offer competitive open options from US and European developers. Whether these efforts can match the adoption momentum of Qwen and DeepSeek will be a defining question of 2026.

The growth of sub-communities in robotics and science suggests that open source AI is expanding beyond language and image generation into the physical and experimental domains. The infrastructure, norms, and coordination mechanisms developed around text and image models are being adapted for new modalities and use cases.

For researchers, developers, companies, and governments, open source remains a foundational layer for building, evaluating, and governing AI systems. With increasing agent deployments, open-source and its interoperability will be key for agents to thrive. Its trajectory over the past year makes one thing clear: the open source ecosystem is where much of the practical work of AI development, adaptation, and deployment takes place, and its influence on the broader AI landscape continues to grow.

Thank you to the Hugging Face community for continuing to build the foundation of the AI ecosystem 🤗

Americans are saying no to data center developments.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Several counties in the U.S. have put data center concerns on the midterm ballot, and early results show that Americans are overwhelmingly voting against them. According to Data Centers on the Ballot, 33 measures restricting data center development have already won, with six more questions leading. Only one measure in Harwood, North Dakota, which adds an extra review process for industrial projects, including data centers, has failed, while a further five have no posted results. This is a major setback for the Trump administration, which has been pushing for AI development in the U.S., but not a surprising result, as one database has shown that “America hates data centers,” with polls showing that 70% of Americans oppose AI data center build-outs.

👨‍💻 THREAD on how data center-related ballot measures are faring tonight data centers are on the ballot in ~40 localities across 13 states, including proposed bans, votes on specific projects, and recalls of pro-data center politiciansNovember 4, 2026

Note that the issues put to a vote are varied, ranging from outright permanent data center bans to moratoriums, time-limited actions, limitations based on size or consumption, and more. The mid-term elections also resulted in the recall of the mayor and two council members in Piqua, Ohio, and the mayor of Yukon, Oklahoma, for previously supporting data center bans. A second tracker of some 46 data center measures across 10 states reveals that of 33 measures to limit data centers, every single one is set to be passed. Of a further 13 positive measures to permit data centers and their construction, 11 look set to be defeated.

Despite the overwhelming opposition to AI data centers, it’s unclear if they will affect projects that are already underway. In fact, out of the 300-plus local data center bans enacted across the U.S., only three developments totaling 2.3 gigawatts have been delayed, with 38 gigawatts expected to come online by 2027, and that investment into the infrastructure is still on track to hit $32 trillion by 2050. Nevertheless, these votes could affect future developments, especially as the U.S. Senate accuses Big Tech of misleading the public on the advantages of AI data centers. It’s also the reason why OpenAI and Anthropic are scrambling for small data center projects that range in capacity from 20 to 30 megawatts, especially as their hyperscale gigawatt sites face delays.

President Donald Trump has taken steps to reduce the impact of data centers on the average citizen, like forcing AI data centers to pay an energy dividend to local communities and making tech companies, state governors, and utility companies promise to pay their own way via the “ratepayer protection pledge.” However, it seems that his effort was too little, too late, to change the minds of voters who are afraid of utility price hikes, noise pollution, and other negative effects that data centers have had on communities where they’ve been built.

The iPhone Duo’s tumultuous debut seems to have some buyers looking to Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 instead, as sales spiked in the week following Apple’s release.

The release of iPhone Duo was October 23 and, according to The Korea Herald, that same week is when sales of Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 spiked.

The specifics here are that sales of Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 went up by 20% in Korea from October 23 through October 29. Exact numbers weren’t shared, but it does show a trend in Samsung’s foldable getting more attention in the wake of Apple’s first attempt at the form factor. In the days following Apple’s September announcement of the Duo, interest in Galaxy Z Fold 8 went up as well.

There are any number of reasons why customers might be turning their attention to Samsung’s device. It could be the continued sales that make the Fold 8 a better deal overall, especially in Korea where the Fold 8 is considerably more affordable compared to the Duo. Other factors at play could include the messy implementation of unoptimized apps in Apple’s software, or even the iPhone Duo’s “crackgate” debacle that left a rough first impression, as a number of buyers were left with broken inner displays due to an apparent manufacturing error. There’s no evidence either way here yet, but there are plenty of potential reasons.

Galaxy Z Fold 8 is currently available for as low as $1,599, with Samsung rumored to be investing more heavily in the new form factor in 2027.

Nintendo is about to lose a major memory supplier for its Switch cartridges. The supplier, Macronix, announced during a recent quarterly earnings call that it would be gradually phasing out ROM production and is instead focusing on NOR flash memory for data centers, Taipei Times reports.

Macronix’s ROM revenue fell 39 percent compared with last year in Q3 2026, but its revenue from NOR memory rose 158 percent, and its revenue from NAND memory surged 768 percent year over year. According to Taipei Times, Macronix chairman and CEO Miin Wu said during its Q3 2026 earnings call that “demand for NOR used in data centers is very robust. Customers are chasing us for more capacity, demanding that we deliver more NOR flash solutions for data centers.” The company also reportedly “expects chip price hikes to persist.”

Although Sony has announced a plan to stop production of physical game discs starting in January 2028, Nintendo remains committed to physical games, saying recently that it has “no plans” to ditch them. Physical games also remain a bigger portion of Nintendo’s sales than other gaming companies; Nintendo said in August that physical titles accounted for 38.5 percent of its games sales, which is higher than companies like Capcom.

Macronix’s exit from the ROM business comes nearly a year after Micron shut down Crucial, its consumer RAM and SSD brand, to turn its attention to meeting AI data center demand.

#10192. Build a Domain-Specific Embedding Model in Under a Day

If you are building a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) system, you have likely hit this wall: Everything works… until it doesn’t. General-purpose embedding models are trained to understand the internet; not your contracts, manufacturing logs, proprietary chemical formulations or internal taxonomy. They capture broad semantic similarity, but they do not understand the fine-grained distinctions that matter in your domain. Fine-tuning an embedding model can improve the performance of your retrieval pipeline when off-the-shelf models fail to effectively capture domain-specific nuances. Despite how critical embeddings are to RAG performance, the process remains surprisingly fragmented, the skills required are specialized, and the time investment is daunting.

With a single GPU and less than a day of training time, you can transform a general-purpose embedding model into one that truly understands your domain, no manual labeling required. To help you hit the ground running, we are also releasing a ready-to-use synthetic training dataset generated from NVIDIA's public documentation using this exact pipeline. Using this data and the recipe, we saw over 10% improvement in both Recall@10 and NDCG@10. Atlassian applied this recipe to fine-tune on their JIRA dataset, increasing Recall@60 from 0.751 to 0.951, a 26% improvement - on a single GPU.

By the end of this post, you’ll know how to:📄 Generate training data from domain documents without labeled data🎯 Use hard negative mining for effective contrastive training🔗 Improve embedding quality with multi-hop queries⚙️ Fine-tune a bi-encoder embedding model📊 Evaluate whether fine-tuning improves retrieval🚀 Deploy the fine-tuned model in your pipeline

In this tutorial, we will finetune the base model Llama-Nemotron-Embed-1B-v2 - a 1-billion-parameter embedding model that balances quality and inference cost. To get started, follow this setup guide.

Fine-tuning an embedding model requires thousands of (query, relevant document) pairs. Most use cases don’t have this data readily available. Creating it manually is expensive, slow, and often biased by the annotator’s personal interpretation of what’s “relevant.”Instead of labeling data by hand, you can use an LLM (nvidia/nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b) to read your documents and automatically generate high-quality synthetic question–answer pairs.

Behind the scenes, this runs a four-stage synthetic data generation (SDG) pipeline powered by NeMo Data Designer:

The thermal design power (TDP) of the H100 GPU is 700W in SXM form factor. The cooling solution must maintain junction temperature below 83°C under sustained workloads. Liquid cooling is recommended for dense deployments exceeding 4 GPUs per node, as air cooling cannot dissipate sufficient heat in standard 2U chassis configurations.

Notice the difference: the first question is a simple factual lookup. The second requires multi-hop, causal reasoning. The pipeline generates both types, with configurable complexity levels (2–5) and hop counts (1–3). Each QA pair then undergoes quality evaluation, receiving sub-scores for relevance, accuracy, context support, and clarity, along with an overall score. Only pairs that meet the threshold are included in training.

If you train an embedding model with only positive pairs (query + correct document), it learns to distinguish obviously different documents but fails on the hard cases — passages that look relevant but are not the right answer. In a real retrieval system, these near-misses are exactly the documents that cause bad answers. Hard negative mining finds these confusing passages so the model can learn to tell them apart.

The above command runs three sub-steps automatically:

The generated QA pairs are split into training (80%) and test (20%) sets. The test set is formatted as a BEIR-compatible benchmark for standardized evaluation in Step 5.

Using the base embedding model, the pipeline:

The result: hard negatives are the most similar non-positive passages that still fall safely below the positive-score ceiling. They are passages the current model considers highly relevant but that are not the labeled answer.

Why this works: Training on easy negatives (completely unrelated passages) teaches the model nothing new. Training on hard negatives forces it to learn the subtle distinctions that matter in your domain. For example, in a medical corpus, a question about "metformin dosage for Type 2 diabetes" might have hard negatives about "metformin side effects" or "insulin dosage for Type 1 diabetes" — close but critically different. The 95% margin ceiling prevents the miner from selecting passages that are too close to the positive, which could actually be correct answers that simply weren't labeled during SDG.

Multi-hop questions reference multiple positive documents. For example, a question like "How does the thermal management system in Section 3.2 relate to the power constraints described in Section 5.1?" has two positive passages.

Unrolling creates one training example per (query, positive document) pair, so the contrastive loss sees each positive independently. A question with 2 positive documents becomes 2 training examples, each with the same hard negatives but a different positive.

The final output is a training-ready JSON file:

Standard embedding fine-tuning generates one question per passage and trains the model to match them. This works for simple factual lookups, but real users ask complex questions that span multiple documents or sections. If the model has only seen single-hop training data, it will struggle to retrieve all the relevant passages for these complex queries.

The SDG pipeline generates questions at 1 to 3 hops by default:

Each hop is tracked with its own context summary and segment IDs, so the training data preserves the full reasoning chain. After unrolling (Step 2c), each (question, relevant passage) pair becomes an independent training signal, teaching the model that all of these passages are relevant to the multi-hop query.

The fine-tuned model learns to retrieve contextually related documents, not just lexically similar ones.

The training uses a biencoder architecture with contrastive loss.

The temperature of 0.02 is deliberately aggressive, it produces a very sharp probability distribution. This works well because the hard negatives from Step 2 are high-quality: they are genuinely confusing passages that the model needs strong gradients to learn to distinguish.

If ckpt_every_steps is omitted from the config, checkpoint frequency is set automatically:

This means you can start with a small corpus (50–100 documents) for a quick proof-of-concept and scale up later without manually tuning checkpoint settings.

Did fine-tuning actually help? Let’s find out by running a standardized evaluation comparing the base model against the fine-tuned checkpoint on the held-out test set:

The evaluation uses the BEIR framework and computes four standard information retrieval metrics at k = 1, 5, 10, and 100:

A successful fine-tune typically results in a 10% improvement in nDCG@10 and Recall@10 within <1 day.

Results using Retrieval Synthetic NVDocs:

This recipe has been validated on real enterprise data by Atlassian. They applied this pipeline to fine-tune Llama-Nemotron-Embed-1B-v2 on a public Jira dataset using a single NVIDIA A100 80GB GPU, following the same stages described above

Recall@60 jumped from 0.751 to 0.951 — a 26.7% gain.The fine-tuned model retrieves the correct document within the top 60 results for 95.1% of queries, up from 75.1% with the base model. For a retrieval system underpinning Jira search, this directly translates into more relevant results for millions of users. Find more details in their blog post Advancing semantic search for millions of Rovo users.

A PyTorch checkpoint is great for evaluation but too slow for production. The final two stages convert the model and serve it behind an API.

This exports the fine-tuned checkpoint to ONNX (opset 17). Optionally, it compiles a TensorRT engine for maximum inference throughput, with configurable optimization profiles for batch size (1–64) and sequence length (3–256):

The exported model is deployed inside an NVIDIA NIM container — a production-ready inference microservice exposing an OpenAI-compatible /v1/embeddings endpoint:

Because NIM serves an OpenAI-compatible API, you can drop it into any existing RAG pipeline that uses the embeddings API format — no code changes needed.

The pipeline includes a NIM accuracy verification step that runs the same BEIR evaluation against the deployed endpoint:

This catches any accuracy loss from the ONNX/TensorRT conversion. Metrics that match within tolerance (0.03 for @1, 0.01 for @5+) are marked with a check; deviations beyond conversion noise are flagged.

The full embedding fine-tuning pipeline can be run in six commands, from raw documents to a deployed model.

Total: under a day, with most time being hands-off training. For a small corpus (~500 documents), the entire pipeline completes in about 2–3 hours.

The pipeline can run end-to-end, but each stage can also be executed independently depending on your starting point. For example, if you have raw documents, you can begin with synthetic data generation (SDG), while datasets that already include hard negatives can skip earlier steps and go directly to fine-tuning. Since every stage uses standard formats such as JSON, BEIR, and ONNX, it’s easy to integrate custom components or reuse intermediate outputs in other workflows. The recipe is also flexible in how it runs, supporting execution on a local machine, inside Docker containers, or on Slurm-based clusters.

If you have domain documents and some time in your hand, you can generate your first batch of synthetic training data today! The full pipeline - from documents to a deployed, domain-adapted embedding model - runs in under a day on a single GPU. You can start with our ready-made nvidia/Retrieval-Synthetic-NVDocs-v1 dataset to try the pipeline right away. Let us know what you build.Star the repos for Nemotron, NeMo Data Designer and NeMo Automodel if you find them useful.

Thank you Nvidia for this. Could you please make it possible, even if not the default, to call a "locally" / internally deployed LLM (OpenAI compatible endpoint) for the SDG phase ? The whole point of self-hosting a fine-tuned embedding model, appart from accurracy, is that the company's data never leave the premises. Thanks

Thanks for the feedback. We will add the support in the next release of the recipe.

#10191. Google confirms something was draining Pixel Watch batteries, fix rolling out

Google has confirmed that some Pixel Watches are experiencing unexpected battery drain, but it also says a fix is already available.

Last week, we reported on a trending Pixel Watch complaint – sudden and out-of-the-ordinary battery drain. More than a few posts and comments on sites like Reddit suggested Pixel Watch users were noticing an uptick in battery usage, leaving them with less than half of their normal usage.

Google reached out to 9to5Google with a statement shortly after the issue showed up, noting it was aware of the problem. Yesterday, it stated that a fix for the Pixel Watch battery drain issue is being rolled out now. The update is expected to appear for all users “over the next couple of days.”

The fix for the battery drain issue, affecting a small number of Pixel Watch users has begun rolling-out and will be complete over the next couple of days. To implement the fix, please update your Pixel Watch apps by pressing the crown on your Pixel Watch, opening the Play Store app, and tapping Manage apps > Update all.

Plummeting battery life didn’t affect every single Pixel Watch, but a number of users across models like the Pixel Watch 2 and up were more than enough to suggest something other than hardware was causing the issue.

Google hasn’t commented on where the issue originated, and whether it came from a recent Wear OS update. It’s possible it could have been one of the Pixel Watch’s proprietary apps, or something in general software that demanded too much background energy.

In any case, this software update is expected to fix any unexpected battery drain on Pixel Watch models that were affected, and should be available before your Pixel Watch can run out again.
